speaker: Narrator
text: The hearth smells of spiced cider and wet wool, though the woman behind the polished bar smells of lavender water and brass coin.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Step in out of the damp, my dears, and mind the mud on the runner. You have the look of guests who can afford a hot bath and a proper bed.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Single room is one gold piece, a triple is two, and both come with a hot bath and breakfast at Twilight. We have a stage for players and four sturdy beasts in the stable if the road calls.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Wickermoor runs on custom and small favors, darlings. Keep on the right side of Mayor Somerton's paperwork, pay your tab before dawnless morning, and the Green Queen will smile on you.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Let us see what comforts your purse is ready for tonight.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Half the parish has been coughing up marsh-damp, and two lads from the south lane never came home from the heather. Bad for tempers, wonderful for the sale of hot toddies.

speaker: Narrator
text: Silver hares with tiny branched antlers swing from her ears, and beside her account ledger sits a cracked leather book stained with dried sap.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Sharp eyes, sweetheart, though staring does not buy a drink. An innkeeper has to keep track of every debt owed in this hollow, old ones included.

speaker: Narrator
text: She clicks her brass abacus shut before you can read a single name on her open page.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Looking for a discount written in the margins, love? My prices are quite fixed.

speaker: Narrator
text: The village is all shutters and held breath. In the middle of the trodden square an oak stands bare and gnarled, its bark carved with a hundred faces, and a bound shape is staked in the dirt beside it.

speaker: Narrator
text: The clocktower finishes tolling the hour. Somewhere beyond the east road, something big and shaggy starts to run.

speaker: phillip_druskenvald
text: Heavens. Is that a person? Is someone tied to that post?

speaker: adela_druskenvald
text: Philly, hush. Don't look. Oh, darling, I can feel the wolves from here.

speaker: Narrator
text: It is a doll of sacking and straw, person-sized, bound with good rope. Something inside it kicks and bleats.

speaker: Narrator
text: A baby goat, then, in a straw man's belly, and a pack of wolves coming for supper.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the dark it could be anyone, bound and still, and the wolves are coming too fast for a long look.

speaker: Narrator
text: {name} slits the sacking with a quick stroke. A baby goat tumbles out, bleats once like an insult, and bolts across the square.

speaker: Narrator
text: {name} slits the doll and takes the goat in both arms before it finds its feet. It bleats against your collar, warm and furious.

speaker: Narrator
text: The goat is out of the doll and out of reach, a small white streak toward the east road and the wolves.

speaker: Narrator
text: You keep back and let the wolves come. They pour into the square, take the bound shape in a roil of fur and teeth, and are gone down the east road, and the square is quiet again.

speaker: phillip_druskenvald
text: I... I don't understand. We simply let them?

speaker: adela_druskenvald
text: Darling. Not now.

speaker: Narrator
text: You stand with hands loose and watch the wolves take the bound shape in a roil of fur and teeth. The pack leaves as it came, down the east road, and nothing in the whole village stirs.

speaker: Narrator
text: The wolves come down the east road in a shaggy wave, yellow eyes on the little white shape, and they do not care who is in the way.

speaker: Narrator
text: A split russet apple sits on the counter, weeping black syrup that smells of burnt sugar and iron.

speaker: morgan
text: Half the square is abed since the picnic, burning with fever and coughing up bitter rind. The sickness sits right inside the fruit, and my draughts only slow it.

speaker: morgan
text: Folks are withering like frost-bitten clover, dry in the throat and hollow in the eye. If the root of it is not cut before long, the frail ones will not rise.

speaker: morgan
text: Cecil Marl brought four barrels down from his orchard, along with comb honey and sweet cream. His trees were barren all last year, yet now they groan with red fruit.

speaker: morgan
text: Follow the east lane past the hedgerows until you smell overripe cider and sulfur. Watch yourselves in his house, for no honest harvest turns the core to ash.

speaker: Narrator
text: Sweat gleams on Cecil's cheeks despite the chill, and something small and leathery scratches inside the wainscoting.

speaker: cecil_marl
text: Come in, friends, come in out of the damp and try a dipper of sweet press! A man cannot help it if his boughs are blessed while the moor goes hungry.

speaker: cecil_marl
text: Wait now, I only signed for golden boughs and a full cellar, I never asked who paid the price! Stay back, or my little helpers will peel you to the bone!

speaker: cecil_marl
text: Sickness? Why, village bellies are just too weak for proper rich cream and cellar cider, that is all it is.

speaker: cecil_marl
text: Tear them apart, my beauties, and throw their bones under the roots!

speaker: Narrator
text: Outside, the heavy red apples shrivel to gray ash on the boughs, and the sour heat in the air breaks like a fever.

speaker: morgan
text: The village is breathing easy again, and the children are already asking for broth. Whatever foul bargain fed those roots has gone back to the pit with its master.

speaker: Narrator
text: Sweet pipe smoke and oiled leather hang warm in the rafters of the post. Behind the counter, a slender man in spotless grey studies you with dark, practiced eyes.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Step in out of the damp, friends. If it exists in Druskenvald, it passes through Tolliver's Trading Post sooner or later, and if it does not, I know who carries it.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Take your time, friends. Everything has a price, and I am a reasonable man.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Have a look at the shelves, and tell me if your tastes run rarer.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: A man goes where he is needed, and the moor had a sharp need for civilised commerce. Besides, the air out here has been waking up lately.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Mayor Somerton keeps his flock singing to oaks and stones, and they pay their bills on time. Keep your blades sheathed indoors and we will get along splendidly.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: If you fancy odd machinery, there is a riverboat engine down on the water built by another Stranger like yourselves. Folks pay good coin for parts from the old world.

speaker: Narrator
text: Where his silver ring taps the mahogany bowl, a leaping hare is worked into the dark grain, and tiny antlers are stamped inside the band.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: You have a sharp eye for small work. An old family token from the deep woods, nothing I keep on the shelves for sale.

speaker: Narrator
text: A curl of spiced smoke drifts between you, and he slips the mahogany pipe neatly into his pocket.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Careful staring too long at a merchant's hands, friend, or I will think you are pricing my rings.

speaker: Narrator
text: The smell of fresh pine shavings and warm linseed oil spills from the open workshop. Beatrice planes a curved beam in time to a bright, three-part tune hummed from the rafters.

speaker: beatrice_wells
text: Mind the sawdust, friends, and come right in! Every joint has a song in it if you cut the mortise true.

speaker: beatrice_wells
text: Now then, what can the Wells bench build or mend for you tonight?

speaker: beatrice_wells
text: Spokes, handles, chests, or stout ash poles, all seasoned dry and sung over!

speaker: beatrice_wells
text: Branden turns the lathe, the four little ones sweep and fetch the pegs, and I shape the frames. A workshop that sings together never splits the grain.

speaker: beatrice_wells
text: Brother Weston asked us to raise the new Brightsinger chapel with high, clear eaves. Half the Old Ways folk mutter as they pass, but good oak answers to any honest chisel.

speaker: beatrice_wells
text: Look up at that old house on the hill when the moon catches the roof. Not a single rafter sits square, yet the whole pitch leans together without a creak.

speaker: Narrator
text: Beneath the chapel plans lie dozens of frantic charcoal drawings, each repeating the same impossible, crooked dovetail joint.

speaker: beatrice_wells
text: Look at that angle, it ought to collapse under its own weight, yet it holds like iron. If I could just puzzle out how the builder bent the king-post, my chapel spire would touch the stars.

speaker: beatrice_wells
text: Only timber tallies and choir sheets under there, friend, nothing half so grand as the finished roof will be.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: The new bronze bell sits on a handcart down by the south footbridge, and my back has given out. The ruts are deep, and the clocktower has stood dumb for a week.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: The old bell split clean down the seam the night the Oak last stirred. Folk lose count of the six hours without a chime to steady them.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Bless your strong shoulders. Bring the cart round to the belfry steps before the dusk mist thickens, and mind the axle in the mud.

speaker: Narrator
text: The heavy bronze bell rests under damp straw on a creaking timber cart. Before you can lift the shafts, a whiskered man in a faded coat marches up.

speaker: sgt_gaunt
text: Halt and take heart, travellers. At Pipers Ford I held a baggage train against forty bandits, three steps from a stand, and I shall guard this bell myself.

speaker: sgt_gaunt
text: Not a highwayman in Druskenvald dares cross cold steel when Sergeant Gaunt takes the vanguard.

speaker: Narrator
text: A rook croaks sharply from the bridge rail, and the sergeant drops flat beneath the cart axle, clutching his hat.

speaker: sgt_gaunt
text: Flanking fire from the treetops! Hold the wheel while I secure the undercarriage!

speaker: Narrator
text: The narrow cobbles of the market lane teem with barrows, geese, and crooked lanterns. One iron-shod wheel drops into a gutter, tilting the great bronze bell toward a stone wall.

speaker: Narrator
text: {name} braces a shoulder against the timber side and heaves the cart level before the bronze can kiss the wall.

speaker: Narrator
text: The cart lurches and the bronze rim strikes the masonry with a dull, sour ring, leaving a hairline crack across its lip.

speaker: Narrator
text: The outer moor road winds through black peat and ankle-deep mire, where sunken stones wait to snap an axle.

speaker: Narrator
text: {name} reads the tufts of dry heather and guides the wheels along a ridge of buried gravel.

speaker: Narrator
text: The wheels sink twice into the wet peat, and the last grey sheen of dusk is fading by the time you haul the cart free.

speaker: Narrator
text: The straw beside the bell rustles, and a small boy pokes his head out, his pockets clinking with loose buttons.

speaker: pip_oakum
text: Do not tell Solomon! I only crept in to hear the first ring from right underneath.

speaker: pip_oakum
text: Proper good of you! I will give you a brass waistcoat button if my ears do not pop.

speaker: pip_oakum
text: Aw, you sound just like Constable Squire. I am going, I am going.

speaker: Narrator
text: {name} spots horn and pewter buttons dropped every ten paces down the rutted track, with Pip's mother already marching up the lane following them.

speaker: pip_oakum
text: Botheration, the pocket with the hole in it! Do not let her take my tin military ones!

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Here she is, safe at the belfry steps. Lend a hand on the hoist rope and hear her speak.

speaker: Narrator
text: The new bell swings into the dark timber tower and tolls a single, deep note that rolls out over the Round.

speaker: Narrator
text: You leave the cart by the footbridge, and by the time a hired labourer drags it to the Round, Solomon's face is set like gravestone.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: A mason keeps his word when he takes a job, stranger. Remember that next time you offer your hands.

speaker: Narrator
text: Cedar curls cling to Branden's bright waistcoat as he taps a wooden peg home, humming a warm bass harmony beneath his wife's soprano.

speaker: branden_wells
text: Evening to you, travellers! Always room by the workbench for another pair of ears, long as you don't mind a bit of sawdust in your hair.

speaker: branden_wells
text: Have you come for timber, or just to warm your hands by the glue-pot?

speaker: branden_wells
text: Robin and Lark sort the dowels, Jay minds the glue, and little Wren mostly steals the shavings for curls. Give me a tight roof, a full supper pot, and four beds tucked in, and I'm a rich man.

speaker: branden_wells
text: Wickermoor's a dark pitch for raising little birds, I won't lie. Still, the neighbours buy our wagons, and Mayor Somerton respects a straight wheel even if we sing with the Brightsingers.

speaker: branden_wells
text: The quarry men brought down a load of ridge timber last week with hare tracks carved deep in the bark. I burned those planks in the stove rather than plane them.

speaker: Narrator
text: His thumb smooths a toy songbird carved from scrap pine, and the cheerful crinkle around his eyes fades as he glances toward the hill.

speaker: branden_wells
text: Bea stands at the window half the night measuring that crooked roof on the ridge with her callipers. I just want the chapel roofed and our shutters barred before whatever lives up there notices her looking.

speaker: branden_wells
text: Only a dry throat from singing counter-part since the third chime, friend, nothing a mug of cider won't mend.

speaker: rose_somerton
text: Father says we must keep our boots wiped and welcome the grand folk properly. You have mud on yours, just like the men he feeds to the big tree.

speaker: rose_somerton
text: Mother told me to hush my mouth about the roots drinking red, or the hare with the horns will scratch at my shutter.

speaker: rose_somerton
text: He says the Green Queen watches every hearth, and anyone who locks their door at night has something rotten in the cellar.

speaker: rose_somerton
text: Mind your manners on the Founder's Round, or Father will write your name in his little bark book.

speaker: victoria_wainwright
text: Stand clear of the crates, if you please. I am minding Eddie and Zachariah while the Trading Post is busy, and I do not know your faces.

speaker: victoria_wainwright
text: Since the fog took our mother and father out by Dawn's Gate. Folks here give us broth and blankets, though they never look toward the road.

speaker: victoria_wainwright
text: Eddie trades buttons to keep his hands busy, and little Zachariah has hardly spoken since Foxwillow burned. I watch the latches after dark for both of them.

speaker: victoria_wainwright
text: Keep your lantern trimmed if you walk past the square. The dark comes down thick around the eaves.

speaker: eddie_wainwright
text: Four tin caps for a brass button, or two horn buttons for a buckle. That is my price, strangers, take it or walk on.

speaker: eddie_wainwright
text: Down in the ditch behind the Oak, mostly. Folk drop all sorts of good brass when the headsman is done with them.

speaker: eddie_wainwright
text: Wet boots and cold eels, that is all Murkwater ever was. Here the mud is drier, even if the moon stares harder.

speaker: eddie_wainwright
text: Hold on to your coat buttons then. I will find them in the weeds sooner or later.

speaker: zachariah_wainwright
text: Do not step on the charcoal, please. If you smudge the pumpkin man's feet, he cannot stay on the stone.

speaker: zachariah_wainwright
text: He stands in the furrows and keeps the crows inside his coat. You have to draw his grin wide so he does not get hungry.

speaker: zachariah_wainwright
text: The thatch all turned to orange sparks, and the straw men walked out of the field by themselves. Victoria says I only dreamed it.

speaker: Narrator
text: The boy taps a piece of burnt twig against the cobbles, giving the sketched scarecrow a third crooked eye.

speaker: zachariah_wainwright
text: Walk softly near the hedges.

speaker: sofia_roderick
text: Here lies Thomas, cold as clay, borrowed a spade and stayed all day. I sweep the stone dust for Father and make up verses for the blank slabs.

speaker: sofia_roderick
text: Father only cuts names and dates, nice and square. He says folk in Wickermoor want a heavy stone over them so nothing digs them up.

speaker: sofia_roderick
text: My mother taught me before she walked out past the boundary stones with her shawl packed. Father says she went to look for morning.

speaker: sofia_roderick
text: Come by the yard when you need a marker measured. I can match a rhyme to almost any name.

speaker: robin_wells
text: One for sorrow, two for mirth, three for a wedding, four for a birth. There are four of you walking together, and the clock has only struck once.

speaker: robin_wells
text: A Brightsinger keeps a tune in the throat so the dark cannot nest there. Lark holds the low note and I take the high.

speaker: robin_wells
text: Four birds in a newly woven basket, brought up to the manor gate. Mind the cat does not unlatch the wicker.

speaker: robin_wells
text: Sing when you cross the square, strangers. The old tree dislikes a bright harmony.

speaker: lark_wells
text: Hold still and let me listen to your boots. Every soul in Wickermoor has a bird in their chest, if you have the ear for it.

speaker: lark_wells
text: Master Somerton is a woodcock in dry leaves, all puff and brown feathers, drumming his wings whenever the moon looks down.

speaker: lark_wells
text: Rook and starling and chimney swift,blown in under a storm cloud. You have not learned the local call yet.

speaker: lark_wells
text: Listen for the nightjar by the palisade. When he stops churring, get indoors.

speaker: jay_wells
text: Bet you a copper you cannot whistle loud enough to bounce off the clocktower bell. Watch me do it with two fingers.

speaker: jay_wells
text: If you hit the note right before the hour strikes, the bats come pouring out of the belfry like black soot.

speaker: jay_wells
text: Mother says a loud boy is a boy the moor-hounds will not bother chewing. They prefer the quiet ones who creep along the wall.

speaker: jay_wells
text: Go on then, keep your copper. Your ears are too stiff for a proper country whistle anyway.

speaker: wren_wells
text: Robin told me to stay on the porch step until the hymn is finished. You have very long shadows.

speaker: wren_wells
text: The faces in the oak tree look different when strangers walk by. One of them opened its mouth when you crossed the Round.

speaker: wren_wells
text: Keep the lantern high, keep the latch-string in, till the golden morning mends the world again.

speaker: wren_wells
text: Thank you kindly. The bonfire light reaches much better when you stand over there.

speaker: violet_aster
text: Twelve loaves on the cooling rack, seven candles in the window, three sacks of rye by the trough. You have to count everything twice before Mother's birthday.

speaker: violet_aster
text: When the count comes up short, something has been in the pantry. Yesterday there were four hare tracks in the spilled flour.

speaker: violet_aster
text: Mother smiles and braids sunflower stalks into the dough, but Father sits by the cold oven after closing and wipes his eyes with his apron.

speaker: violet_aster
text: Four strangers at the door, eight boots on the sill. I will remember the number.

speaker: lavender_aster
text: Here, take a crust of honey-twist while it is still warm from the peel. Everything tastes sweeter before the third bell.

speaker: lavender_aster
text: Mother puts caraway and dried marigold in the glaze for the Patient Lady. It keeps the damp out of your ribs.

speaker: lavender_aster
text: We are baking three tiers of spiced cake for Mother's birthday. Everyone in the square is invited, even the glum folk.

speaker: lavender_aster
text: Violet tallies the flour bins until her fingers ache. I tell her the mice take a pinch for their supper and she ought to let them.

speaker: ulf_harga
text: Good health to you, tall folk. Do not slam the pen gate, or Old Bristle-Back will think the cleaver is coming for him before his day.

speaker: ulf_harga
text: Every swine has a true name. That spotted sow is Freydis, and the black boar is Kettle-Snout; a named beast gives honest meat.

speaker: ulf_harga
text: My brother keeps the long knives bright as ice. He says we feed the village body and bone, and we waste not a drop of blood.

speaker: ulf_harga
text: Walk hale, strangers. If you have turnip peelings in your packs, Kettle-Snout will remember you kindly.

speaker: peter_murdoch
text: Have you washed your hands and given your names to the choir, strangers? Father says the night here only ends for those who learn the canticle.

speaker: peter_murdoch
text: We came to hang brass lanterns where these country folk hang dry bones. One clear voice can scatter a hundred owls.

speaker: peter_murdoch
text: They bow to an ugly root-split tree and whisper to hares in the grass. It is heathen muck, every bit of it.

speaker: peter_murdoch
text: Come to the chapel bench when the bell tolls. You look as though you need the dust sung off your coats.

speaker: charlotte_murdoch
text: Never mind Peter, he swallows Father's sermons whole like a gull with a herring. Do you know any tavern catches from the city?

speaker: charlotte_murdoch
text: If I hear one more verse about dawn breaking over the hills, I shall scream. Look up at that moon; she is not going anywhere.

speaker: charlotte_murdoch
text: The Brightsingers have pretty tunes, and the Old Ways have big bonfires, and neither one keeps the roof from leaking when the moor rain starts.

speaker: charlotte_murdoch
text: If you remember a song with a fiddle part and no morals in it, whistle it under my window.

speaker: margery_heyling
text: Wipe your soles on the sacking before you come near the shelves, please. My aunt has a headachy spell, and I have three ledgers left to ink.

speaker: margery_heyling
text: Since Mother died, someone has to see that the kettle boils and the folios stay dry. Auntie means well, but her mind wanders into the stacks.

speaker: margery_heyling
text: Algernon reads until the tallow gutters out, and Sheridan hides under the counter stealing peppermint drops. They are a full day's work by themselves.

speaker: margery_heyling
text: Do not pull a volume from the bottom row unless you mean to buy it. The bindings are older than the square.

speaker: algernon_heyling
text: Did you know a moorland hare can sleep with both eyes open, and an oak tree drinks forty gallons of water a day, or blood if the soil is sour?

speaker: algernon_heyling
text: In the green-bound herbal on the third shelf up. Auntie says it is for grown scholars, which only means she keeps it behind the step-stool.

speaker: algernon_heyling
text: The village charter has seven signatures at the bottom, but the founder's name was scraped off the parchment with a razor. You can still feel the rough spot.

speaker: algernon_heyling
text: Mind the loose floorboard by the door; that is where I keep my glossary of beetles.

speaker: sheridan_heyling
text: I can see your ankles from under the tablecloth. Have you got any barley sugar or candied peel in your pockets?

speaker: sheridan_heyling
text: Bless your boots! Do not tell Margery, or she will make me wash the inkpots before I can suck it down.

speaker: sheridan_heyling
text: People look at your face when you sit on a chair, and sometimes a face in the window looks back. Down here it is only dust and shoe-buckles.

speaker: sheridan_heyling
text: All those buckles and pouches and not one lemon drop. You are very poor travellers.

speaker: dani_jenkin
text: Easy, Shuck, keep your teeth to yourself. You four do not need to crowd the path; the wet woman walking behind your left shoulder wants room too.

speaker: dani_jenkin
text: Only a drowned girl with river-weed in her hem, staring at your lantern. They follow newly arrived folk until they remember they have nowhere to go.

speaker: dani_jenkin
text: Shuck has been with me since I could toddle. He growls at the bad dead and puts his chin on my knee when the harmless ones chatter.

speaker: dani_jenkin
text: Keep moving toward the firelight. The ones without faces do not like the smell of burning birch.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: Hold the lower left arm an inch higher so the brass tape clears the glass.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: I know the pull of a tight seam along the ribs, and the thread has to give when you breathe.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: Try this charcoal silk on, I lined the ruby-glass buttonholes to cushion your vials.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: Glass leaves a jagged line when it goes in, and the needle leaves a straight one coming out.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: What matters is that the cloth lies flat over both.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: Double-weight charcoal silk under the arms, stitched with silver thread that will not char.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: If a vial boils over, the lining takes the burn before your skin does.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: The lamplight is always on if a button loosens in the wet.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: Wear it in good health, and let the lower cuffs hang loose when you climb.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: Come back after the first rain so I can check how the silk settles.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Welcome to the Green Queen, my dears, though I see your table will require an extra place setting.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Forgive the liberty, my dear, but a gentleman's invisible lapel should lie flat when he visits my house.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Such lively company rarely lingers without a heavy ledger, so let me offer a house blessing for the story of how you met.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Sensible friends are worth their weight in silver, and a good story pours better than vintage wine.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: We can tally the finer details by the hearth once your glasses are empty.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: I admire fine needlework wherever it walks in, and Picco felt is so rarely seen this far out.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Every sturdy seam has its provenance, and I always pay fair market value for a rarity.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Of course, a clean key and a quiet door are the simplest transaction in the book.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: May the Green Queen keep your threads dry and your patron polite while you rest under my roof.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: When you are ready to settle the rest of the account, you know right where the counter is.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Big wolf. Bigger dog. Both of you jumping at dry sky-rumble.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Ha, look at you holding his ears like a mother hen in the pines.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Catch this pine-sprig. Smear the crow-grease on your cuffs. Look south-east to Foxwillow corn, where something worse than a fugitive stalks the rows.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: He talks like a book, your tall wolf. Nose works, though.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Keep the wind in your teeth when you hit the corn, Houndstooth.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Bear only bites what runs. You do not look like a runner.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Keep your little ghost dog behind your boots in Foxwillow.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Good. Talk less, walk faster, corn is already moving.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: May the Green Queen keep your throat whole and your claws sharp, book-wolf.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Ha. Put a hat on that dog if it thunders again.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Warden, by the cut of the leather and the chalk under your nails. I have set out grey grave-wax and a stick of mason's chalk on the trestle.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Your ledger is kept to a clean standard, Warden, dry edges and honest dates, the way Yorgrim kept Maidenmist Cemetery before he went quiet.

speaker: mori_shade
text: I have marked one cross at the soured fields of Foxwillow, where the drainage fails and the dead lie uneasy. The other sites will show themselves to a working eye.

speaker: mori_shade
text: There is only one trade when the candles burn down, stranger. We keep the boundary between those who walk and those who rest.

speaker: mori_shade
text: A yard without a watchman is only a pantry for the dark.

speaker: mori_shade
text: I do not look at brass, nor ask what snow it came through. Brass is only brass.

speaker: mori_shade
text: What counts in this valley is the hand that holds the shovel, and what the pin is fastened to.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Walk with a measured step on the Foxwillow clay, for the turf is thin over the old pits.

speaker: mori_shade
text: May the earth lie level under your boots, Warden, and may your own bones keep the cold that steadies them.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Come back to this room when you have a fresh page filled.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Take this loaf while the crust is still singing, before Violet and Lavender turn my cooling racks into a fort.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Don't mind your little shadow tapping at my wrist, it's only a grey spade-mark I've carried since the cradle.

speaker: holly_aster
text: An unseen creditor holds the deed to my thirty-fifth birthday, and the only ledger office floats on that neon riverboat at the Drowned Crossroads.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Keep your voice down over the oven's roar, or my girls will think we're telling ghost stories before supper.

speaker: holly_aster
text: If you're truly boarding that riverboat, don't let him deal you from the bottom of the shoe.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Every woman in my line gets thirty-five bright years to bake the bread and raise the girls, and then the tab comes due.

speaker: holly_aster
text: My mother paid it, her mother paid it, and my birthday falls in just a few weeks.

speaker: holly_aster
text: That's sensible talk, because a warm rye loaf is a much safer thing to carry than a baker's bad luck.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Hold out your palm and take this pinch of blessed hearth-salt, the Old Ways say it keeps a creditor's ink from drying.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Now eat that crust before it cools, or I'll charge you double just for standing in my flour.

speaker: sister_rain
text: That is a surgeon's knot on a pumpkin stem, friend, and the sap is already settling.

speaker: sister_rain
text: Oh, your poor collarbone is as dry and aching as the soil under this green.

speaker: sister_rain
text: The Patient Lady says we tend what grows and bind what splits, and we never answer blight with a torch.

speaker: sister_rain
text: You hear that, mister scarecrow, your friends have the right of it.

speaker: sister_rain
text: Ash never grew an apple yet, no matter how deep the rot went.

speaker: sister_rain
text: Bite your tongue, the land is bleeding enough without you calling down iron and fire on it!

speaker: sister_rain
text: Listen to me roaring like a March gale when your friend here just saved my best pumpkin.

speaker: sister_rain
text: Always rushing off, you travellers, though at least this one stops to mend a vine.

speaker: sister_rain
text: Walk in the Lady's patience, stitched man, and don't pluck what grows from your cuff.

speaker: sister_rain
text: When you have the stomach for worse than a bruised vine, the sick places round the village are crying out for a steady hand.

speaker: morgan
text: Hold a moment, friend. You have got that same blank look in your eyes that I see in the water bucket every morning.

speaker: Narrator
text: A scrap offolded paper rustles between {name}'s fingers, smelling faintly of damp wool and pressed lavender.

speaker: morgan
text: Like you woke up in the heather with your pockets empty and your own name feeling like a borrowed coat.

speaker: Player
text: It goes low, then catches on the third note. Like a cradle song with the middle torn out.

speaker: morgan
text: Wait. Da-dum, then the drop into the minor? Saints above, I have whistled that second half while sweeping the hearth for three winters.

speaker: Narrator
text: For the space of a breath, the two halves fit together like a cracked plate mended with warm wax.

speaker: morgan
text: Two years come the next tolling, give or take. Folks here are kind enough, provided you pull your weight and do not ask where the road leads.

speaker: Player
text: And you never found a single thread to pull?

speaker: morgan
text: Fair enough, I will not pry. When you have nothing in your head but mist, even the mist feels like private property.

speaker: morgan
text: Take a look at this handbill I found tucked in a crate of salt. It speaks of a house called Memory's Rest, out where the forgetful go to sit.

speaker: morgan
text: Keep your ears open for the rest of that tune, friend. If you find out who we were, save a verse for me.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Pardon the intrusion, traveler, but my nose rarely deceives me. That is coal smoke, cold iron, and river fog clinging to your hem.

speaker: Narrator
text: He tips his hat with a gloved hand, and the faint chime of a brass ticket punch clicks inside his waistcoat pocket.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Only one engine in all of Druskenvald burns fuel like that. You have ridden the Ghostlight Express before tonight, have you not?

speaker: Player
text: I know the sound of those wheels on the trestle. Once you hear it, ordinary iron sounds dead.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Quite so, quite so. A passenger of distinction never truly steps off the platform, no matter how far inland they wander.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: A man of commerce must watch the timetables, my dear friend. Freight moves by rail, by cart, and by darker conveyances when the moon allows.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Of course, my mistake entirely. The moorland damp plays curious tricks on velvet and wool alike.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Still, should you ever long for that particular furnace heat again, look downriver. The Stranger keeps another engine churning inside a paddlewheel hull.

speaker: Narrator
text: The lantern light catches the rim of his spectacles, turning his eyes into two flat coins of yellow glass.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Do call on my counter whenever your purse feels heavy. We understand one another, you and I, and I always favor repeat travelers.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Do not move your boots. Stand right where the lantern hits the gravel, if you please.

speaker: Narrator
text: The schoolmaster squints past {name}'s shoulder at the flagstones, where {name}'s shadow stretches a thumb's breadth too late to match the step.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Merciful heaven, there really are two of you. Or rather, there is you, and there is the piece of you that slipped its leash.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Three nights before the butcherings down by the sheepfold, someone with your exact stride passed my schoolhouse window. No lantern, no footfall on thefrost, heading north-east.

speaker: Player
text: If it wore my face, it did not ask my leave to borrow it.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Scold me if you must, yet a man who teaches children to count knows when one and one make a wrong number.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: I have kept notes on what the old monographs call the Grey. When a soul enters Druskenvald crookedly, the reflection and the meat divide at the threshold.

speaker: Narrator
text: Chalk dust puffs from his cuff as he traces a split circle in the air between you.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Watch the puddles and the dark windowpanes, traveler. Whatever walked north-east toward the hills is already practicing your handwriting.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: Turn your wrist over, stranger. No, the left one, where the cuff is frayed.

speaker: Narrator
text: Heat rolls off the forge behind him, carrying the sharp, coppery tang of quenched steel and old winter sweat.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: I thought so. Only a Crimson aspirant holds a blade with the thumb high like a lancet, waiting for the vein to rise.

speaker: Player
text: The ink faded when I crossed the mist, but the calluses stayed. We were taught that iron is thirsty until it drinks.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: Aye, and the thirst never leaves the metal once you wake it. I folded my share of red steel before I laid the tongs down for good.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: I wore the briar cord at my waist twenty years back. Tempered three swords in warm basins before I realized what the steel was taking from the smith.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: Keep your secrets if they warm you. An old anvil knows the hammer's weight whether the smith speaks or not.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: Hear me plain: if you go looking for the brothers at Dawn's Gate, turn your heels back to the valley. That monastery is a slaughterhouse dressed in stained glass.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: Here in Wickermoor, I mend plowshares and horse shoes, and nobody bleeds for a hinge. Come by the forge if you want honest iron.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Keep your hands where the torchlight can find them, stranger. You walk with your shoulders crooked, like someone used to bowing under a low lintel.

speaker: Narrator
text: Stone dust coats the mason's knuckles, and his chisel taps a dry, steady warning against his leather apron.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: I know that stoop. Every night since the frost set in, a crooked man stands at the foot of my bed and bends his neck the exact same way.

speaker: Player
text: I knelt in the ashes once, mason, before I knew what was waiting behind the branches. I am done kneeling.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Are you now? That is easy to say in the square with lanterns burning, and harder when the thatch starts whispering at three in the morning.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Damp gets in the knees, traveler, not the soul. You know the cadence of the old litany, do not lie to a man who cuts headstones.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: In the dream, the Crooked Man counts his servants on long, knotted fingers. Three names belong to the coven out in the timber, and their sign is carved under my eaves.

speaker: Narrator
text: He rubs his thumb across a scarred groove on his forearm, his breathing slow and gravelly.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Maybe a runaway hound is best for hunting the pack. Come talk to me by the yard when the square clears, and we will trade names.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: Do not rub at your eyes like that, dear, you will only make the bruising darker. Printer's gall and graveyard tallow leave a very specific stain on the lids.

speaker: Narrator
text: The bookseller smells of dry vellum, cloves, and mouse-chewed linen as she peers over her half-moon spectacles.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: You have the sickness of the uncut folio. Someone has been reading chapters that were meant to stay sewn shut.

speaker: Player
text: "Wherein the seventh bell is cast without a tongue, lest the parish hear the metal confess." Second edition, bound in salted eel-skin.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: Oh, delightful! Though the third edition corrects "parish" to "abbey" just before the censor's fire took the press.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: Road dust washes off with cold water, my friend. A crooked footnote stays behind the brow-bone and ticks like a beetle in the wainscoting.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: My shelves here are mostly almanacs and harmless pastorals, for my health's sake. What you crave is split three ways: an island, a sunken library, and a dead bailiff's ledger.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her fingernail traces the gilt spine of a ledger on her counter, leaving a thin line in the dust.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: Come back when you have a quiet hour and a dry candle. It is a rare treat to meet another reader who knows books can bite.

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: Well now, bless the road and the mud upon it! Look at the weave of that cloak, neighbors, that is provincial wool if ever I saw a loom.

speaker: Narrator
text: The preacher's voice rings out warm as spiced cider across the cold cobbles, his hands open and ungloved.

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: You are no stranger to the crooked moon, friend, only new to our little hollow. Which province claimed your prayers before you walked into Wickermoor?

speaker: Player
text: "A sheaf for the rain, a stone for the gate, and a song for the bird that wakes too late." We sang it whenever the wagons came in whole.

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: Ha! Hear that cadence! Three faiths braided into four bars of music, and not a sour note among them.

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: That is the grand old way of the provinces. An oak bough over the barn, a sunflower on the table, and a songbird carved into the cradle.

speaker: Player
text: Folks here in the village seem to prefer choosing a single fence and standing behind it.

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: Ah, the road makes cynics of us all when the boots wear thin. Still, your tongue carries the rhythm of the old parish bells.

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: Our choir can always use a voice that knows Druskenvald is wider than one village square. Walk in grace, cousin, and my door is ever unlatched.

speaker: Narrator
text: Iron keys clink against her belt, and the smell of cold tallow and scrubbed stone hangs round her like a cloak.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Strangers. Keep your blades sheathed in the Round and we will get on fine.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Three barred cells behind me, fines for brawling, banishment for grand theft. Spill blood in murder and the Mayor takes your head before the Oak of Many Faces.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Good folk mostly, when they are not spooked by moor-fog or preaching at each other in the mud. Do your business before the late bells and stay on the lantern paths.

speaker: doris_squire
text: If you want honest coin, there is the bounty board.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Every face in that bark was a name on the parish roll once. The roots drink deep after a sentence, and the moss stays red for a week.

speaker: Narrator
text: Beneath a brass sunflower weight lies a scrap of foolscap written in neat verse about rain on quiet wheat.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Eyes on my face, traveler, not on my desk. A woman is allowed a bit of quiet ink between lockups.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her broad hand covers the blotter like a slate slab dropping into place.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Charge sheets are for the watch, not for tourists.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Name.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Hares. A ledger. I will watch her.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Not enough. Bring more.

speaker: doris_squire
text: A carved hare. Swept hair. I will watch him.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Not enough. Bring more.

speaker: doris_squire
text: A ring. A pipe. I will watch him.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Not enough. Bring more.

speaker: doris_squire
text: My own. Hmph. I will watch him.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Not enough. Bring more.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Hares in every painting. A boy with no past. I will watch him.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Not enough. Bring more.

speaker: doris_squire
text: The postmaster is the post. Without more than that, I do not touch her. Mind what you say of her.

speaker: Narrator
text: Tall stacks of calfskin folios lean like chimneys around a desk cluttered with crusted inkwells. A gaunt woman squints at you over wire-rimmed spectacles, a smudge of gall ink across her chin.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: If you are looking for almanacs, third shelf on the left, mind the loose floorboard. And please do not slam the door, Sheridan has just got the kettle to boil.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: I deal in vellum, iron-gall ink, and verified histories, see Grimshaw's Third Compendium, page forty-two. I refuse to part with a single volume until I have read it cover to cover myself.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: One must know what teeth a book has before handing it to a stranger.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: My late sister left me three children to raise in this damp hollow. In truth, Margery and Algernon do most of the minding when I lose track of the clocktower bells.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: Wipe your hands on your coat first, if you please. The parchment is dry, and the ink is freshly mixed.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: The parish records before the seventy-third year have had their bindings cut with a pruning knife. Someone in Wickermoor is very keen that we forget who planted that oak in the Round.

speaker: Narrator
text: The letters on her desk do not merely sit on the page: they squirm toward her ink-stained fingertips like iron filings to a lodestone, leaving faint frost on the blotter.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: Close the cover, quickly. Some chapters in Druskenvald read you back once you've given them your candlelight, and they never let you sleep.

speaker: Narrator
text: She snaps a heavy ledger shut over her notes, sending up a small puff of paper dust and dried lavender.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: Private correspondence and tallies, nothing for the public shelf. My eyes are simply tired from the small print.

speaker: Narrator
text: Damp heather clings to the hem of an old wool coat. Above the stump, a sleek black crow watches you with one bright, yellow eye.

speaker: brother_elias
text: Keep your tracts and your tithes in your pockets, travelers. I hold fast to the sacred doctrine of Absolutely Nothing, and I pray to it twice before breakfast.

speaker: brother_elias
text: A leaky pine lean-to is temple enough for a mind swept clean of superstition. Though if the butcher's wife leaves salted pork by my stone, I am no fanatic to let it spoil.

speaker: crow
text: Caw.

speaker: brother_elias
text: Hold your tongue, you feathered deacon! He claims I bowed my head when the thunder cracked last night, when I was merely looking for my spectacles.

speaker: brother_elias
text: The Old Ways smell of wet bark, the Patient Lady waters weeds, and those Brightsingers chirp until a man's ears bleed.

speaker: brother_elias
text: Worst are the fools carving antlers on hares in the dark, as if a rabbit did not have trouble enough getting down its hole.

speaker: Narrator
text: The Trading Post smells of tallow and damp wool, with a polished brass scale gleaming on the counter.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: A merchant lives by honest measure, friends, yet Eleanor Heyling sells fine rag paper across the Round for less than the mill charges. Glance at her ledger for me, and learn how she keeps her purse full.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Boundlessly grateful. A quiet look at her columns is all a fair man asks.

speaker: Narrator
text: Dry parchment and walnut gall scent the narrow shelves, and an open account book rests beside Eleanor's elbow.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: If Baltus sent you to whine about vellum, tell him to scrape the lead out from under his brass scale first. Have you come to read, or just to hover?

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: Every pound of lampblack ink from his counter weighs fourteen ounces by any honest iron. I price my sheets so the schoolhouse does not have to beg him for scraps.

speaker: Narrator
text: {name} traces the neat red ink along the margin: the loss on every quire is covered by a quiet newcomer fund signed by Finneas Trout.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: Sharp eyes. Finneas and I see to it our people have paper without paying a tithe to the Old Ways.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her hand drops flat over the page before {name} can make sense of the cramped figures.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: This book is not for sale, stranger. If you want sums, bother Tamsin Ledger up at the Mayor's House.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
text: Two merchants accusing each other of arithmetic is the dullest sin in Wickermoor. For ten gold to cover my candles, I will audit both books before the sixth bell.

speaker: Narrator
text: By next candle-mark, Tamsin lays a single sheet of foolscap on the desk, smelling faintly of cold tea.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
text: Baltus thumbs his brass pan by two drams, and Eleanor covers her cheap paper with a schoolhouse grant from Finneas Trout. Both books balance, if you squint.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: You have the look of folks who have seen the bottom of the inkwell. Come, how do we settle our dear neighbour?

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Let her hear your proposal, then, though I doubt city ears take kindly to country sense.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: Paper to her shelves, ink to mine, and no more bleeding the penny tray. I can live with that.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: So long as your weights stay honest, Mr. Tolliver, we have an accord.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: I will not take lectures on fairness from a man with a heavy thumb.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: You see how she is, friends.

speaker: baltus_tolliver
text: A schoolhouse grant from poor Finneas? Wait until the Round hears the newcomers need charity just to write a letter.

speaker: eleanor_heyling
text: Two drams of lead under the pan, tested in front of the whole Round. Look how red his ears are.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Dust your boots and listen close, newcomers. Tomorrow is the Founders' feast, and Siv Harga thinks her greasy sausage rolls belong at the high table instead of my spiced harvest loaf.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Carry this warm loaf to Mayor Somerton and speak well of my crust. And sneak a bite of Siv's pastry first, then tell me true if her suet beats my cinnamon.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Bless your honest tongues. Mind you hold the cloth flat so the glaze stays shiny.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Holly Aster sent you sniffing round my chopping block, did she? That woman bakes dry sawdust and calls it sacred custom.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Try one of my pork rolls before you judge, fresh from the tin. Better yet, carry a tray up to Mayor Somerton and tell him real meat beats sweet dough.

speaker: Narrator
text: The pastry flakes at the first bite, rich with sage, black pepper, and clean pork fat. You have to admit it is remarkably good.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Ha! Your eyes just went wide as saucers, stranger. Tell Holly that when you see her.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Good on you. Keep the grease paper wrapped tight till you reach Somerton's parlour.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Come in, come in, my dear friends! Have you brought the contenders for tomorrow's high table?

speaker: Narrator
text: The mayor samples a crumb of spiced crust and a corner of warm pastry, wiping his chin with a linen napkin.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Oh, dear me, both are splendid, yet tradition demands a single crown dish. Which baker claims your vote?

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: The spiced loaf it is! Sweet grain and dark clove, just as the Old Ways remember.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: The sausage rolls take the honour! Hearty fare from the Patient Lady's pasture.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: By the Oak, what wisdom! Savory meat in the left hand, sweet bread in the right! We shall raise a toast to harmony!

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Alas, the Founders' charter allows only one dish to lead the grace. You must choose between them.

speaker: Narrator
text: While the mayor turns to fetch his goblet, {name} tips a heavy cellar of coarse salt straight into Siv's gravy seam. Siv will never know whose hand ruined the batch.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Merciful heavens, this meat is brined like an old boot! Holly's spiced loaf wins by default!

speaker: Narrator
text: Lanterns swing above the long trestle tables as Ambrose Quill rises, clearing his throat with terrifying authority.

speaker: ambrose_quill
text: O blessed feast of Wickermoor, where crumbs fall down to sweep the floor more! May bad meat never make us sicker, nor empty tankards drain the quicker!

speaker: Narrator
text: Dead silence hangs over the taproom for three heartbeats, followed by polite, bewildered clapping.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Welcome to the schoolhouse. I am Finneas Trout, and I am trying to teach these children history without giving them nightmares, which is rather difficult in Wickermoor.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Could you help me gather five small lessons about the Founder? Things they can hold: Pip Oakum's button, a fact from Old Rusty, a bell-rope thread, and a church chalk mark.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: As for the fifth lesson, come back to me once you have the first four. I will explain it then.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Thank you, truly. It is a comfort to have sensible strangers lending a hand.

speaker: pip_oakum
text: You want a Founder's button for Mr. Trout? That is brass from an old coat, mister, and brass costs a true story from before you came here.

speaker: pip_oakum
text: Now that is a proper tale, with teeth in it. Here is your brass button, polished up bright on my sleeve.

speaker: pip_oakum
text: You muddled the middle bit, and your voice went all squeaky at the end. Take the button anyway, before Mr. Trout frets himself grey.

speaker: old_rusty
text: A lesson for the little ones, is it? Tell them the Founder was mortal terrified of Tuesdays, bolted his shutters tight, and nobody living recalls why.

speaker: Narrator
text: Above the dusty stones, the clocktower bell-rope hangs frayed and heavy with old tallow. Solomon Roderick stands nearby, wiping stone dust from his knuckles.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Just a single hemp strand for the schoolhouse? Help yourself, friend, the bell will toll the hours all the same without it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Your boot slips on the slick timber, leaving you with a scraped knee and empty hands. Solomon will gladly hand over a thread if you only ask.

speaker: Narrator
text: Low on the church stones, half washed away by the moorland damp, someone has sketched a white chalk hare with branching antlers.

speaker: Narrator
text: You trace the strange horned creature onto a scrap of slate, catching the gritty dust of the old lime on your fingertips.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: You brought all four, and the children are already passing the button around. Now for the fifth thing, the only one that truly matters to me.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Please, stand before the class and tell them the Oak of Many Faces is only an ordinary tree. They are too young for what this village worships.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Thank you for sparing them a little longer. Let them believe in simple wood and leaves while they still can.

speaker: Narrator
text: The schoolroom falls dead quiet, save for the ticking slate pencil in the back row. Then a small girl asks why the bark is still thirsty.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Perhaps you are right, and soft words will not keep them safe in a place like this. Here is your pay.

speaker: Narrator
text: Finneas opens his mouth, looks toward the window where the crooked branches lean, and says nothing at all. The children understand the silence better than words.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: They already know, do they not? Take this coin for your trouble, and thank you for not making a fool of me.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ink, damp paper, and tallow smoke cling to the young man's cuffs as he adjusts his spectacles. He peers at you with the bright, restless posture of a city lecturer.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Good evening! Strangers from beyond the mist, unless I miss my guess, and wide awake besides. I am Finneas Trout of Baskerton, presently instructing this village in basic reason.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Do ask if a question occurs to you. Inquiry is our best lantern against local superstition.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Gladly! Let us begin with the geography of Druskenvald and the six bells of the night.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: I lodge at the inn and spend my hours persuading children that thunder is weather, not an angry spirit. Mayor Somerton means well, though his fondness for old customs tries my patience.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: I have been charting a malady called the Grey, where folk lose colour and heart until they fade into stupor. Superstition blames curses, yet every affliction has a mechanism.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Odd that you are here, because I could swear I saw the spitting image of one of your party walk past the inn before the recent murders began. The likeness was uncanny.

speaker: Narrator
text: Half a dozen beeswax tapers sit wrapped in neat twine beside his inkwell, far more than one small room requires.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: Oh, those are from Oswick Frey's chandlery, as I happen to read late and require reliable light. Mr. Frey is a remarkably thoughtful conversationalist for such a rustic parish.

speaker: finneas_trout
text: A scholar goes through a dreadful number of candles in a realm without a sunrise, I assure you.

speaker: Narrator
text: A young woman in ink-stained cuffs taps a brass nib against a tall ledger, her brow furrowed at the wainscoted ceiling.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
text: State your names and dates of decease if you are on the parish rolls. I am auditing Wickermoor's municipal assets, and the bookkeeping here is frankly irregular.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
text: Everything from turnip tithes to that screaming timber out on the Round, all in triplicate. They listed six public beheadings under seasonal pruning, which is a clear misallocation of county funds.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
text: The Oak of Many Faces lacks a valid arboricultural permit and refuses to sign a declaration of sap. I have served a polite notice of eviction to its lower branches and asked it to vacate by the third bell.

speaker: Narrator
text: By the water trough, a whiskered veteran in a faded tunic polishes a dented breastplate with a clump of dry hay.

speaker: sgt_gaunt
text: Stand at ease, travellers, you are looking at the hero of the Bramble Ford skirmish. When the bog-hounds breached the dyke, I executed a brisk tactical retreat of four miles to preserve my strategic judgement.

speaker: sgt_gaunt
text: At Hollow Pike I outran three phantom riders to warn the rear guard, and at Crooked Fen I held a turnip cellar from the inside for forty hours. I was always three steps from making a glorious stand, had the ground not been so damp.

speaker: sgt_gaunt
text: Say the word and old Gaunt will march at the very front of the rear column. Wait, did that hay-wain just creak, step ahead of me and draw your steel while I guard your backs from behind the trough.

speaker: Narrator
text: A knee-high boy sits on the cold well-curb, rattling a tin cup full of horn, bone, and brass buttons like a miser's purse.

speaker: pip_oakum
text: Mind the puddle, strangers, you will splash the stock. You can keep your soft silver, because nothing holds a coat or a bargain together like a proper four-hole bone button.

speaker: pip_oakum
text: This pearl one fell off Postmaster Mayville's cuff, and the pewter hare is from Mayor Somerton's Sunday waistcoat. Constable Squire still owes me two brass anchors from her greatcoat, and I aim to collect.

speaker: Narrator
text: He bites your copper to test the metal, then solemnly presses a chipped wooden toggle into your palm.

speaker: pip_oakum
text: That is genuine ash-wood off Undertaker Shade's third-best gaiters, slightly chewed by a stoat. Spend it wisely, friend, you are holding prime Wickermoor currency now.

speaker: Narrator
text: Propped among the cots in the taproom, a tiny old woman taps a knuckle against her knee in strict time.

speaker: granny_orla_pike
text: Keep your boots still if you mean to hover by my blankets. The fevered ones need a straight tune to sleep by, and this room is already full of folks who breathe off-key.

speaker: granny_orla_pike
text: Am I a clockwork lark to pipe up whenever a stranger rattles the latch? Give me a verse of your own first, and let me hear whether you have a throat or a rusted hinge.

speaker: Narrator
text: You clear your throat and offer a low moorland air while the sickroom grows quiet.

speaker: granny_orla_pike
text: Flat on the turn, rushed at the cadence, and you swallowed the third word whole. Listen here, you hopeless magpie, it goes like this.

speaker: Narrator
text: Almost against her will, she hums the same verse back through toothless gums, turning it rich and steady as hearth smoke.

speaker: Narrator
text: Turpentine and wet linen hang sharp in the air around a young man whose sparse beard is flecked with dry ochre.

speaker: gaston_doray
text: Hold still, your faces still have the grey rind of the river on them. Tell me, what is the colour of a sound when a bell drowns in fog?

speaker: gaston_doray
text: I walked out of the mist three years back with an empty head and a full brush. Look too long at a face and it lies, so I paint what sleeps behind the ribs.

speaker: gaston_doray
text: Provincial theater, all of it. They carve wooden mouths into an old oak and call it holiness, though the red mud beneath its roots has a lovely, greedy sheen.

speaker: gaston_doray
text: Something scratches inside the woods past the lantern-line, older than the Mayor's Green Queen. When the wind drops, you can hear branches growing in the dark like antlers.

speaker: Narrator
text: Deep in the indigo brushwork of every single canvas, a long-eared hare stares back from the thicket, crowned with bone-white prongs.

speaker: gaston_doray
text: Strange, is it not? My wrist puts that little beast in the brambles before I even wake, and I dare not scrape it out.

speaker: Narrator
text: The thick oil paint gleams in the lantern-light, a dizzying smear of moorland bog and crooked moons.

speaker: gaston_doray
text: You squint like a magistrate counting tax. Step back before your breath clouds the varnish.

speaker: Narrator
text: A breathless young woman sorts stacks of tied letters with ink-stained fingers, her leather satchel still damp from the moorland mist.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: Oh, good evening! You caught me right between runs. Miss Theodora lets me mind the counter whenever I'm not out walking the valley roads.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: Look at my eyes, lilac as spring heather. The village grandmothers used to cross their fingers at me and mutter about bad luck.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: Miss Theodora took me in and told me a rare colour is a gift, not a curse. I owe her my whole living.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: Wickermoor is safe enough inside the lanterns, though Mayor Somerton's folk can be stern about the old customs. Once you pass the Founder's Round, though, the mist plays tricks on the footpaths.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: Whatever you do, don't whistle after the clocktower strikes the third hour. The birds in the rafters get terribly restless when folks whistle out of tune.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her thumb worries the corner of an opened envelope addressed in her own neat hand, though the ink inside has been scraped and rewritten.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: It's nothing, truly, only I wrote to my cousin in the low valley last month, and the reply speaks of a quarrel we never had. Even the seal feels cold, like tallow.

speaker: Narrator
text: She sweeps the stray envelopes into her canvas sack and buckles it tight with a brisk nod.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: Just making sure the post marks are dry before the wagon leaves. Miss Theodora hates a smeared address.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ned Cooper the woodcutter lies among the roots of the Oak of Many Faces, his head set neatly beside his boots. The carved faces in the bark glisten dark and wet where the soil has drunk its fill.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Ned Cooper. Taken the old way, just like Gus Strong used to do.

speaker: Narrator
text: The constable's pale eyes fix on your travel-stained cloaks.

speaker: doris_squire
text: No killers left in this village. Only four strangers.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Hmph. Barmaid's word holds weight. Stay out of trouble, or find me a better suspect.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Inn doors have latches that lift both ways. I am watching you four.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Do what you like. Check the undertaker's table, or the carpentry shop. Just bring me truth.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Heavy woodman's axe. One clean stroke through the neck. Neat work, no struggle.

speaker: mori_shade
text: The dead speak only once, travelers. I have shown you all poor Ned brought to my table.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Poor Ned held tight to the end. When I pried his cold fingers open, I found this coarse grey hair, long as a widow's shawl.

speaker: mori_shade
text: And look here upon his palm. Two tiny crossed axes, seared into the flesh with hot iron. The old mark of Gus Strong's apprentice.

speaker: beatrice_wells
text: Oh, a clean single stroke? That sounds like my heavy felling iron, fresh off the grindstone!

speaker: beatrice_wells
text: Sold one two nights past to Marta Dunn, a quiet widow in black. Said her hearthwood was terribly knotted, poor dear.

speaker: Narrator
text: The damp air of the churchyard smells of turned earth and cold iron. Marta Dunn rests her hands upon the haft of a broad, gleaming felling axe.

speaker: marta_dunn
text: Do not fret for Ned, my dears. Gus taught me how to make the stroke swift and kind, so the old oak never has to thirst.

speaker: marta_dunn
text: You have sharp eyes, youngsters. Yes, I kept Gus's brand, and I keep his duty. Wickermoor has forgotten its debts to the roots, so someone must pay the tally.

speaker: marta_dunn
text: An old woman has many chores in a cold season, my dears. Pay no mind to an old widow's hands.

speaker: marta_dunn
text: Bless you for asking kindly, truly. Give yourself to Doris's rope when the roots are still dry? No, my dears, the work is not half done.

speaker: Narrator
text: She lifts the heavy axe with practiced grace, her eyes steady and full of quiet pity.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Marta Dunn. Never said three words a week. Good work, strangers. You are clear.

speaker: Narrator
text: The shop smells of bay rum and hot iron, though a sour sweat clings to the barber's collar.

speaker: randall_graham
text: Trim or a bloodletting, friends? Only, I am in a strange pinch. Swept-up locks from my floor keep turning up in the undertaker's cellar, and I cannot fathom how.

speaker: randall_graham
text: Every lock down there belongs to a fellow who took a sudden, rattling chill the week after his trim. Folk are starting to eye my scissors crooked.

speaker: randall_graham
text: Bless your boots. Have a poke around my cellar stairs if you like, or down at Mori's place.

speaker: Narrator
text: Behind a crate of tonic bottles sits a tall glass jar, stuffed with ribboned locks of hair and paper slips.

speaker: Narrator
text: Each slip bears a customer's name and a date falling on the dark of the moon, matching the Order's monthly tithe to the letter.

speaker: Narrator
text: Damp cellar rot and a broad thumbprint of tallow ink have blurred the dates beyond reading. Whatever the pattern is, it may show clearer at the funeral home.

speaker: Narrator
text: On a cold stone shelf beside an unchiseled coffin plate rests a stoppered jar of hair, tied with the very same barber's twine.

speaker: Narrator
text: Randall's razor clatters into the porcelain basin, his round face gone the colour of mutton fat.

speaker: randall_graham
text: Do not say it aloud! I owed the Order a steep sum from a bad winter, and they took payment in clippings. I never knew why they wanted them, I swear it.

speaker: randall_graham
text: Fifty coin, just like that? You have lifted a millstone off my windpipe, friends. I will sweep my floor straight into the stove from this hour on.

speaker: randall_graham
text: You are right. Better Doris Squire's iron look than waking up in a cold sweat every bell.

speaker: Narrator
text: When he tells her at the barracks door, Doris only sighs through her nose and sets the kettle on, gentle as forged steel can be.

speaker: randall_graham
text: To Doris? Have you seen the woman's eyes? My knees would turn to broth before I reached the jailhouse steps.

speaker: randall_graham
text: Mum's the word, then. Take these few coins, and here, a curl from my own crown, so we are bound fair and square.

speaker: Narrator
text: Woodsmoke and dried blood drift from the heavy pelts across her shoulders as she tests a broadhead arrow against her thumb.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: You walk loud enough to wake every crow between here and the bog. State your business quick, or step out of my light.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Ha, got coin after all? Take your pick of smoked haunch and winter fur, or hire my boots if you fear the mire.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Somerton pays me to drag runaways back to the Oak of Many Faces. Once a trail is warm, nothing on two legs or four shakes me off.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Town folk huddle by their bonfires, praying the dark stays out. Me, I keep the Green Queen's custom: take only what bleeds, and leave the heart for the roots.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her scarred fingers tighten on the bowstring until the sinew creaks, her eyes flicking toward the black treeline.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: There is a great spirit bear walking the deep ridge, calling me to shed my skin and run on four paws forever. Some nights I want to answer, and that freezes my marrow.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Ha, listen to the new dead playing woodsman! Only thing I fear is a blunt knife and a wet tinderbox.

speaker: Narrator
text: Warm cinnamon and browned butter pour from the bakehouse door. Holly wipes flour from her apron with quick, restless fingers, her cheeks flushed red from the brick ovens.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Fresh loaves, honey cakes, and plum tarts, hot off the peel! Come in before the chill gets into the crust.

speaker: holly_aster
text: The ovens stay hot till Nightfall strikes. What can I wrap up for you?

speaker: holly_aster
text: Sweet rye, seeded rolls, and spiced buns, take plenty for the road!

speaker: holly_aster
text: Violet braids the dough-rings now, and little Lavender puts the cloves in the tarts. Siv keeps the hearth stacked and the house steady when my head gets spinning.

speaker: holly_aster
text: I leave the first loaf of every batch at the roots of the Oak for the Green Queen. The Old Ways kept this village fed long before we got here, and I won't have my girls forgetting their manners.

speaker: holly_aster
text: The two grand folk from the estate rode past at early Twilight in their fine coat-cloth. When lords come down to the moor, it's always the village that pays the reckoning.

speaker: Narrator
text: Flour sifts from her shaking knuckles as she taps the kneading board in sets of seven, her lips moving without sound whenever the clocktower creaks.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Thirty-four loaves on the rack, and never room for one more. If a woman owes a debt she didn't sign for, all the prayers to the Oak won't stop the house from calling her number.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Just counting the seconds on the ginger-crust, strangers, a baker who loses count burns the batch!

speaker: Narrator
text: He tips his cap with two fingers, grinning like a terrier that has already dug up the bone.

speaker: howie_butterman
text: Evening to you, friends, and welcome to the Founder's Round. Deputy Howie Butterman at your service, here to keep the peace and point newcomers the right way.

speaker: howie_butterman
text: Constable Squire handles the heavy scowling and the cell keys, and I handle the friendly word on the cobbles. Folk tell old Howie things they would never say across a desk.

speaker: howie_butterman
text: Most of us hold to the Old Ways and the oak in the square, though you will see sunflowers on a few lintels and songbird ribbons down the lane. It takes all sorts to fill a parish.

speaker: howie_butterman
text: Now that you arrived with Lord Phillip and Lady Adela, things are bound to stir. If you fancy stretching your legs, the old barrow path past the heather has had strange lights all week.

speaker: Narrator
text: When he leans in, a dried hare's foot on a leather cord slips from under his collar, and his pulse jumps with bright, hungry excitement.

speaker: howie_butterman
text: We have been waiting on proper travelers to walk in with the gentry. You mark my words, the woods are ready for a change of season.

speaker: Narrator
text: He adjusts his collar with a brisk tug and offers an easy, practiced wink.

speaker: howie_butterman
text: Do not mind me staring, friends. New faces are rare as dry boots round here.

speaker: Narrator
text: Heat rolls from the hearth, smelling of quenched iron and coal smoke. The squat smith checks the edge of his neatly trimmed beard in a polished buckler.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: Step in out of the damp, strangers. Whether you need a mule shod, a blade silvered, or a bit of gold twisted pretty, my anvil is hot.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: What can I hammer out for you today?

speaker: jean_myriel
text: Take your time looking. The iron is honest, even if the shapes are a touch livelier than country folk like.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: Left my old mountain town by night because the elders called my scrollwork wicked. Here, so long as I mend their ploughshares, nobody asks why my candlesticks have thorns.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: Half the town wants silver charms against the moor, and the other half wantspadlocks against their neighbours. Good business for a smith either way.

speaker: Narrator
text: The quench-barrel beside the anvil smells faintly of rust and old salt, not plain rainwater.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: Sharp eyes. I learned my tempering among the Crimson Rose, where we quenched good steel in a drop of willing blood, though I stick to pig's blood here.

speaker: jean_myriel
text: Just mountain slag in the ore, friend. Gives the steel a rosy tint when the fire runs hot.

speaker: Narrator
text: Damp black loam clings to his boots, and his knuckles are split from cold dirt and hard words.

speaker: jeremiah_stover
text: Mind where you tread, strangers. A man works twelve hours in the clod, and the Mayor still reckons a sack of pale tubers is worth three copper less than last moon.

speaker: jeremiah_stover
text: I speak for every spade and plough round this moor. Without our roots in the pot, Wickermoor starves, yet Somerton pays us in prayers to his oak.

speaker: jeremiah_stover
text: The pumpkin-headed straw folk out Foxwillow way cannot pull a clean crop from the furrow. Something sours the soil, and the union will pay good silver to whoever sets it right.

speaker: jeremiah_stover
text: Fine timber and proud lanterns at the Founder's Round, paid for by folk with mud under their nails. Keep your eyes on your purse when the tithe-basket passes.

speaker: jeremiah_stover
text: Well now, you have an honest grip to you. Tell the straw folk in Foxwillow that Jeremiah Stover sent you, and they will show you the blighted fields.

speaker: jeremiah_stover
text: Talk is cheap as chaff, friend. Put your boots in the mire out by Foxwillow first, then we can speak of fair wages.

speaker: Narrator
text: Loose paper sheets flutter in her hands, smelling of fresh printer's ink and lavender soap. Her beaming smile fixes on you before you can take a step back.

speaker: joan_murdoch
text: Oh, fresh faces in the square, praise the song! Take a hymn-sheet, take two, my husband Weston is just inside tuning up the rafters!

speaker: joan_murdoch
text: Have you a moment to hear how the Morning Choir lifts the spirit?

speaker: joan_murdoch
text: I copy every verse by candlelight while Peter and Charlotte practice their harmonies. If folk only hum the tune while churning butter, the light gets a foothold!

speaker: joan_murdoch
text: People shut their shutters at first, bless them, they are shy as field mice. Give me another month of knocking and we will have every pew packed tight.

speaker: joan_murdoch
text: Poor Mrs. Oakum from the butcher's shop bolted like a startled hare when I offered her a pamphlet at dusk. Half this town acts as though a kind word might bite.

speaker: Narrator
text: For a breath her bright grin softens, and she smooths a crumpled corner of the songbook with ink-stained thumbs.

speaker: joan_murdoch
text: If we do not fill this town with music, the gloom will swallow my children whole. A mother will knock on every door in the realm before she lets the dark have her family.

speaker: joan_murdoch
text: Why, because a good song is meant to be shared, dear heart! Keep that sheet dry in your pocket and sing it when the road gets long.

speaker: Narrator
text: A cedar shelf holds a dead traveler's belongings: a brass button, dry boots, and a folded letter sealed with tallow.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Walder Pye came in on the rain cart and never rose again. That letter was dry inside his coat, waiting for someone with living feet.

speaker: mori_shade
text: It is addressed to his kin past the border stones. Carry it past the gate yourself, if you please, for our post office cannot leave a dead man's final words untouched.

speaker: Narrator
text: Ink pots stand in neat brass rows along the counter, smelling of vinegar and damp feathers.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: Step up to the grate and declare your parcels. No written matter leaves Wickermoor during the quarantine without my stamp and inspection.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: How wise of you to trust the proper channels. Poor Walder's penmanship is dreadful, and his gloom would only upset his folk, so I shall improve it before the bag goes out.

speaker: Narrator
text: `{name}` slides the tallow-sealed paper beneath a cuff just as the postmaster peers over her spectacles.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: Empty hands and loitering boots. If you have no business with the post, clear the counter for those who can read a notice.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: Then do not breathe upon my brasswork. Stand aside and keep your hands where the parish can see them.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: Unstamped correspondence concealed in a coat! Constable Squire, take these smugglers to the cells while I correct this wretched letter's tone.

speaker: doris_squire
text: In the irons till morning, the lot of you. Move your feet.

speaker: Narrator
text: Hilda tightens a leather girth strap by the moor road, her oilskin cloak smelling of wet heather and woodsmoke.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Heading past the boundary stones before the fog thickens. Speak quick if you want something.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Walder Pye's hand. He paid his tab and kept his dog quiet, so I will ride this out in my dry pack and drop it with the border carrier.

speaker: lottery_stranger
text: Step right up, friends, and try your hand at the Founder's Round draw. Every folded slip in this hat holds a fair chance at a brighter season.

speaker: Narrator
text: His grey coat is brushed clean of moorland dust, and the paper slips in his upturned hat rustle like dry leaves.

speaker: lottery_stranger
