text: One hundred gold coins in a neat leather purse, paid on the spot. More than that, the winner enjoys a full year of effortless good fortune.

speaker: lottery_stranger
text: A slip costs ten gold coins to draw from the hat. As for those who do not win, we simply cross their entry from the active roll and move along.

speaker: lottery_stranger
text: Nobody in Wickermoor complains of a bad draw, I promise you that.

speaker: lottery_stranger
text: Ah, an appreciation for tidy bookkeeping. I keep every participant's name in clean black ink so there is never a dispute.

speaker: Narrator
text: Dozens of local names are struck through with a ruler-straight line of wet black ink. When townsfolk pass by, their eyes slide right over those cottages as if no one ever lived there.

speaker: lottery_stranger
text: Forgive me, friend, the damp air smudges the ink if I leave the pages open too long.

speaker: Narrator
text: He shuts the leather cover with a soft, polite thump and tucks the brass clasp into place.

speaker: Narrator
text: The ledger bindings snap in your grip, scattering inked pages across the trodden mud of the square.

speaker: lottery_stranger
text: Well now, that is one way to balance an account. Enjoy the rest of your evening in Wickermoor, travellers.

speaker: Narrator
text: He steps back between two lantern-bearers, and by the time the smoke clears, his grey coat is nowhere to be seen.

speaker: lottery_stranger
text: Ten gold received, and recorded in full. Reach into the hat whenever you are ready.

speaker: lottery_stranger
text: Look at that mark upon the paper. We have ourselves a fortunate soul tonight.

speaker: Narrator
text: The villagers around the square clap and cheer a bit too brightly, their smiles stretched tight in the lantern glow.

speaker: lottery_stranger
text: A blank slip, I am afraid, though I thank you for playing. Let me just tidy the register before you go.

speaker: Narrator
text: His nib draws a single, cold black line through one of your names, and the air around your shoulders turns chill and thin.

speaker: lottery_stranger
text: Entirely your privilege, travellers. Should you find yourselves feeling luckier on another turn of the clock, you know where I stand.

speaker: Narrator
text: He touches the brim of his hat with two gloved fingers and turns back to the crowd.

speaker: Narrator
text: A broken halter dangles from the post, and the damp straw of the third stall is still warm.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: The clocktower tolled and my grey mare Clover bolted straight up the northern moor road. Find her before the wolves do, and you will have my goodwill and three days free horse hire.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: She is gentle as rain, just terribly skittish around flapping cloaks. Hold out a handful of dry oats and she will come right to your palm.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: Mind the ditches out there. The fog hides the ruts, and she has got only one good shoe on her forelegs.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: Empty halter in my hand and wind rising off the heather. Have you seen a hide or hair of her yet?

speaker: marianna_grey
text: Keep your cloaks tucked in and shake a pouch of oats if you get close. If the mud hides her prints, fetch Hilda Brom.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: I see. Best I latch the third stall shut then, and save the clean straw for the horses that are left.

speaker: Narrator
text: Deep, crescent hoofprints score the wet peat along the northern verge, filling slowly with black moor water.

speaker: Narrator
text: Scuffed moss and snapped gorse stems mark a stumbling path toward a dark bramble thicket beside the north wall.

speaker: Narrator
text: The hoofprints vanish into a boggy churn of cart ruts and sheep droppings. Hilda Brom could read this mire better than you.

speaker: hilda_brom
text: Thrown left shoe, panicked stride, dragging her halter rope through the gorse. Look in the thicket by the north wall.

speaker: Narrator
text: The dapple-grey mare stands tangled in wet briars by the stones, flanks heaving and ears pinned back at your shadow.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her trembling eases at your touch, and she lowers her velvet nose enough for {name} to take the frayed halter rope.

speaker: Narrator
text: She snorts in terror, wrenching free of a briar to bolt a few yards down the wall. A handful of oats might steady her where quick hands failed.

speaker: Narrator
text: The dry grain rustles in your palm, and the mare steps out of the thorns to lip the oats from {name}'s fingers.

speaker: Narrator
text: Clover presses her damp forehead against the stablemistress's shoulder, blowing a long, warm breath into her apron.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: Look at you, plastered in peat and burs, you foolish old girl. Take this coin for your trouble, friends, and any horse in my yard is yours free for three days.

speaker: Narrator
text: Warm hay, liniment, and horse-sweat sweeten the dark of the stable, where a broad-shouldered woman braids a mule's mane with steady fingers.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: Mind the grey mare's hind leg, she startles at cloaks. If you need a stall or a mount, say so plain.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: Two silver a night for stabling, brushed and fed right. I sleep up the ladder over the stalls, and a horse never lied to me yet.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: Too much talk in the square about roots and blood for my liking. I keep a dried sunflower by the hayloft door and ask the Patient Lady for dry straw and quiet nights.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: Tell me what beast or tack you have need of.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: The mules come back from the north ditch lathered and shaking, with burrs twisted into knots no bramble ever made. Something out there runs on two legs and smells like winter.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her calloused thumb rubs the branded tag on a bridle, her shoulders softening with quiet gratitude.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: Miss Alda acts sharp with her silver, sure, but she sends hot soup up my ladder when the frost bites and tells me to learn the inn's cellars. I do not know why she bothers with the likes of me.

speaker: Narrator
text: She turns back to the manger and lifts a heavy sack of oats with one arm.

speaker: marianna_grey
text: Miss Alda pays on the hour and leaves my beasts be. That is plenty.

speaker: Narrator
text: A big timber-framed house on the square opens its door, and a round man in a three-piece suit that strains at every button bustles out across the dirt, a cane in one hand and a bowler in the other.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Lord Phillip! Lady Adela! And what a way to be greeted. You have caught us in the middle of a very old custom, I'm afraid, and I do beg pardon for the commotion.

speaker: phillip_druskenvald
text: Mayor. Mr. Somerton, is it? We were told your village was quiet.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Quiet, my lord, quite, but for tonight. The oak drinks from the herds, once a year, so the hunting stays good and the barns stay full. A sacred tradition, nothing more.

speaker: Narrator
text: He mops his bald head with a handkerchief and looks, for the first time, at the strangers who stood by and let the thing happen.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: And you, good travelers, were kind enough to let the rite alone. The Green Queen takes note of respect, and I shall see that the village does too.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Saved the little fellow, did you? Well, well. The oak will drink from the beasts of the field whatever you do, and a goat is a goat. We'll say no more of it.

speaker: Narrator
text: His smile holds, but his handkerchief has gone to his forehead, and he does not stop mopping.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Cut it loose, did you? The rite is the village's, you understand, and the Queen does not forgive a spoiled offering as easily as I do. I shall say a word to the neighbors.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: A blood offering to the Green Queen, who keeps the Hollow's herds and hunts. Tradition, tradition. We've done it since before the clocktower, and the harvests have never once failed us.

speaker: Narrator
text: His eyes slide to the east road and back, and a muscle jumps in his jaw. He is a man hiding something to please a lord.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Er. Some of our people have been, ah, taking sick lately. And a few have gone off without a word. Nothing to trouble his lordship with.

speaker: Narrator
text: He looks like exactly what he is, a mayor with a very good suit and a very full evening.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: The Druskenvald estate is quite ready for you, my lord. Pristine, staffed, a fine gift from the village. And for your friends, the Green Queen Inn, the one decent lodging in the Hollow. Alda Farnum keeps it.

speaker: Narrator
text: The mayor's smile goes thin, and then goes altogether, and under it is a tired man in a tight suit.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: More disappearances, more fevers, more funerals than there ought to be. I'd rather not say more in front of the lord. Come to my office when it is open, and I will tell you what I know.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Oh, I'm sure I don't know what you can mean. A village is a village, good people. It has its seasons.

speaker: phillip_druskenvald
text: Mayor, I do hope you'll forgive us. It has been a long road, and I find I am dreadfully tired. Darling, shall we go up and see this gift of yours?

speaker: adela_druskenvald
text: Oh, swell. Philly, don't pout, the house will be darling. Friends, you'll come to dinner tomorrow, won't you, once we've seen the rooms?

speaker: Narrator
text: Phillip's smile has been put on a half-beat late, and the hand on his cane is white at the knuckles. He is looking at the oak.

speaker: phillip_druskenvald
text: Splendid. Forty gold between you for the inn, on me. The estate, tomorrow evening, and we shall have a grand old time.

speaker: Narrator
text: You watch two small figures, one twirling a cane, walk up the winding path toward the crooked manor on its hill, the windows lit and every line askew.

speaker: Narrator
text: In the round below, the oak's carved faces lie in the moonlight, and one of them, you would swear, turns to watch them go.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: Oh, thank the moon you are strangers! I dropped three unsigned letters into the wrong cubbies, and if Miss Theodora sorts the dead-letter sack tonight, I shall die a second time.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: They were meant for Deputy Butterman. Now one sits on Constable Squire's desk, one went to the undertaker, and the square goat has the third. Please fetch them back.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: Constable Squire has eyes like carpentry nails, and Mr. Shade measures your collarbone whenever you say good evening. If I go near either of them, my knees will turn to suet.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: Bless your boots! Look for lavender paper sealed with a crooked heart, and please do not read the bit about his ears.

speaker: Narrator
text: A square of lavender paper lies beside the constable's inkwell, smelling faintly of pressed violets and terror.

speaker: Narrator
text: {name} slides two fingers across the green blotter, and the lavender sheet vanishes into a coat pocket without a rustle.

speaker: Narrator
text: A boot heel clicks on the floorboards right behind {name}'s shoulder.

speaker: doris_squire
text: "Thine eyes are like two poached eggs in clouted cream." That is either a threat to the peace or poetry, and I lock up for both.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Keep the paper. I will sleep on whether to charge you, and you will sleep in the straw.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Take it. I read it twice to see if it was a cipher from the woods. It is badly spelled. I mean it kindly.

speaker: Narrator
text: The undertaker's parlor smells of cedar shavings and damp wool. Mori opens a narrow drawer lined with velvet.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Unclaimed things come to me sooner or later, one way or another. I kept the lilac note in the third drawer, just in case.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Ah, the living and their little urgencies. Take it along, before the damp gets into the ink.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Paper is light, but keeping secrets takes drawer space. Leave five coins for the ledger and give me a cousin's middle name for my list, and we are square.

speaker: Narrator
text: The tether chain clinks against the founder's stone as the old billy goat works his jaw sideways. A corner of lavender paper sticks out from his beard.

speaker: Narrator
text: {name} scratches behind the goat's horned crown until his yellow eyes half-close, then draws the damp last third of the page from his teeth.

speaker: Narrator
text: The billy goat fixes {name} with a flat yellow stare, gives one final chew, and swallows the last scrap with great dignity.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: One from the desk, one from the parlor, and one mostly inside the goat. At least Miss Theodora will not pin them to the noticeboard.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: Only now I am looking at them, and my courage has gone cold. What on earth do I do about Howie?

speaker: howie_butterman
text: For me? Well now, nobody ever compared my ears to buttercup petals before. I am not sure it is accurate, Miss Geneva, but I am mighty pleased.

speaker: howie_butterman
text: Ma'am, I never knew you had such tender feelings under your truncheon.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Get back on your rounds, Butterman, before I fine you for loitering. And stand up straight.

speaker: Narrator
text: {name} matches the looping clerk-hand at the bottom of the page, signing it simply from a friend in the post office.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: That is neat enough to pass Miss Theodora herself. He will wonder next time he buys a stamp, and that is half the fun.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: Oh dear, the ink has blotted right through the paper. If I send that, he will think a spider died on the page.

speaker: Narrator
text: The lavender scraps curl into black ash over the post office brazier, smelling briefly of cheap scent and sealing wax.

speaker: geneva_fairchild
text: There. Better ash than poached eggs in cream, honestly. Tomorrow I shall buy thick cream paper and write him something sensible.

speaker: Narrator
text: Bundles of dried yarrow and bog-mint brush your shoulders, and glass vials clink softly on crooked shelves. Morgan looks up with faraway green eyes, fingers stained violet with crushed roots.

speaker: morgan
text: Oh, come in, mind the low beam by the door. I was just labelling the willow-water, or perhaps I already finished that an hour ago.

speaker: morgan
text: Was there another draught you needed, or did we only just begin talking?

speaker: morgan
text: The red bottles mend torn flesh properly, and the herb bundles mostly comfort the locals, though comfort does half the curing.

speaker: morgan
text: I have no beds for the sick, only bottles and poultices to carry home. People tell me their aches, and I try to remember which jar eased them last time.

speaker: morgan
text: Everyone in the hollow has an old name and an older grave to tend. Sometimes I wonder what sort of name I had before the moor took me in.

speaker: morgan
text: Some nights I brew tinctures that let a drinker see through mist or hear what the dead whisper in the thatch. I never quite recall who taught me the measure.

speaker: Narrator
text: The open ledger on Morgan's counter has whole pages torn short, with ink trails stopping mid-word as if the hand simply froze.

speaker: morgan
text: Funny thing, the clock strikes one bell and when I blink it is striking the next. I woke here small and alone, and the years between still slip through my fingers.

speaker: Narrator
text: Morgan gently closes the stained ledger under a bundle of dried chamomile.

speaker: morgan
text: Do not mind my messy handwriting, nobody in the hollow can read apothecary scrawl anyway.

speaker: Narrator
text: The parlor smells of beeswax and cold tin. Mori pulls open a shallow cedar drawer filled with gleaming brass coffin plates.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Forgive the clutter, friends. I stencil these for the Order of the Oak, though the folks named on them are still walking the streets.

speaker: mori_shade
text: I truly could not say. On the first of each month, a folded slip and a silver piece wait beneath my door.

speaker: mori_shade
text: A man must keep his fires lit, so I oil my punches and I do not watch the threshold.

speaker: Narrator
text: Five brass plates lie nested in black velvet, each stamped with neat, square letters.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Geneva Fairchild, Howie Butterman, Ambrose Quill, and Finneas Trout. The fifth plate was ordered polished, but left completely blank.

speaker: mori_shade
text: My hands shake more with every letter I strike. You are strangers here, unburdened by our customs: tell me what ought to be done.

speaker: Narrator
text: Word travels the cobbled lanes faster than mist off the moor, leaving shuttered windows and bolted doors behind it.

speaker: mori_shade
text: They cross the mud to avoid my shop now, whispering that the undertaker wishes them cold. Perhaps they are right to fear me.

speaker: Narrator
text: Brass curls and blackens in the belly of the iron stove, filling the small room with a sharp, metallic tang.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Let them come for their silver if they dare. My lungs feel clear for the first hour in a year.

speaker: Narrator
text: Constable Squire turns the paper over once in her gloved fingers, her face as grey and unreadable as slate.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Keep your shop shuttered after the third bell, Mori. I will copy these into the ledger and walk the Round myself.

speaker: Narrator
text: The drawer slides shut with a soft wooden click, swallowing the faint gleam of brass.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Best to let the village sleep easy, I suppose. I will have the oil lamp trimmed before the next slip arrives.

speaker: Narrator
text: A single brass plate rests upon the workbench, newly struck, the metal filings still clinging to the letters.

speaker: mori_shade
text: The monthly note came while you were at that dreadful house, friends. They finally gave me a name for the blank plate, and I thought you should see it.

speaker: Narrator
text: The scent of dried rosemary and freshly turned peat clings to the woman in black. Her white hair gleams like bone under the lantern light.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Step softly, newly arrived. You stand upon ground that has welcomed many before you, and will hold many more before the moon wanes.

speaker: mori_shade
text: When a companion falls in Druskenvald, the soil does not easily let them go. I wash the brow, fold the hands, and pay the earth its proper due.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Old Yorgrim down at the cemetery taught me the spade-work when I first woke here. Every soul deserves a quiet pillow, whatever they were before.

speaker: mori_shade
text: The Mayor's folk feed the Oak of Many Faces with blood, while the Brightsingers try to sing the dark away. I keep to the Strangers' way: we owe the Ferryman a polite nod and a clean ledger.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Tell me whose memory we are tending, and we shall see them properly laid to rest.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Do not pluck the white violets that grow round the base of the Founder's Round. Their roots drink deep from those who died without a name, and they weep on your fingers.

speaker: Narrator
text: She touches the tarnished brass oar pinned to her lapel, her voice dropping to the hush of river reeds.

speaker: mori_shade
text: You know the Vagrant's mark, then. He rowed us all across the dark water once, and he watches still to see if we waste the second breath he gave us.

speaker: mori_shade
text: It is only an old keepsake from the riverbank, traveller. A reminder that every road ends at the water's edge.

speaker: Narrator
text: The parlor goes awful still save for the dry rustle of pages as she turns to a black ledger on the desk, smellin' of cedar and cold tallow.

speaker: mori_shade
text: I do not call the departed back myself. I only go down to the water, ask the Ferryman to turn his oar, and carry him his toll.

speaker: mori_shade
text: He turns his oar only for souls in the water no more than ten days. They return weak and stumbling for ten days, the water's shadow clinging on.

speaker: mori_shade
text: The toll is a thousand gold pieces for each soul I carry to him, whoever they were and however far they came. I keep no gems and ask no other payment.

speaker: mori_shade
text: You will see the toll set out for each companion before anything is paid. Tell me whom you mean to call back to the near shore.

speaker: mori_shade
text: The Ferryman keeps his ledger open, and the offer stands for the full ten days, whenever your purse allows.

speaker: Narrator
text: The lamps burn low in the parlor, and a damp chill settles deep into the quiet room at this hour.

speaker: mori_shade
text: The Midnight and Witching hours I give to the graves, and the Ferryman takes no asking now.

speaker: mori_shade
text: Come back to me from the Twilight Hour until the Evening Hour is spent. The ten days will keep.

speaker: Narrator
text: The tang of cold tallow and wet dog hangs about her apron. She keeps her head down, paring grey fat from a knucklebone with a notched knife.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: If you want prime cuts, talk to the master up front. I only scrape the troughs and haul the bone-bucket out back.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: Speak quick if you need something. The clock don't wait on idle tongues.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: It suits me fine. Folks leave me be, and I get the gristle and marrow-ends to carry home before the Evening bell rings.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: Once that bell tolls, I lock myself out on the high scrub till Twilight comes round.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: Folk here pray to their big thirsty tree and think the hedges will keep the dark out. A fence only keeps in what wants to stay.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: Something foul is seeping out of the Skitterdeep mine, up north-west in the crags. The creek water tastes of copper and bad fever, and the beasts know it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Coarse grey hairs bristle along the scarred skin of her forearms, and her breath catches at the scent of raw liver on the block.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: Keep your eyes to yourself, stranger. A heavy chain and a sack of butcher's offal is all that keeps my teeth out of this town come dark.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: Best not stare at a working woman's hands while she holds a cleaver, friend. Mind your own business.

speaker: Narrator
text: She smells of starch and dried chamomile, her hands folded neat over her apron while her gaze flicks toward the nursery stairs.

speaker: myrtle_somerton
text: Good evening. If you are looking for Wendel, he keeps his hours in the office, though I ask that you keep your voices low near little Rose's door.

speaker: myrtle_somerton
text: Being the mayor's wife means keeping the silver bright and making sure Wendel does not promise the parish away to flatter quality. My real work is keeping Rose at her lessons and indoors.

speaker: myrtle_somerton
text: It is a respectable village when folk mind their own hearths. I tell Wendel that all this fuss over old trees and midnight bells only gives the simple folk bad dreams.

speaker: myrtle_somerton
text: Too many shutters have stayed barred past the third bell this month. The baker's apprentice has a rattle in his chest that no kettle of broth seems to touch.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her knuckles whiten on her apron hem, and you see iron pins driven into the windowsill beside a child's wooden doll.

speaker: myrtle_somerton
text: People do not just wander off into the gorse when they know the paths from birth, no matter what the constable writes down. I bolt Rose's shutters before the first bell, and I do not open them for anyone.

speaker: Narrator
text: She smooths her skirt with a brisk pat and offers a tight, proper nod.

speaker: myrtle_somerton
text: A mother is always careful in damp weather, that is all. The moor air is hard on small lungs.

speaker: Narrator
text: Dark sap weeps from the knots of the old oak as a dozen wooden eyelids creak open in the moonlight. The smell of iron and wet earth rises from the roots, and the carved mouths begin to move together.

speaker: Narrator
text: A dry chorus rustles through the bark like dead leaves scraping across a stone floor. They whisper that their roots are parched, that they are so very tired of the dark, and that the axe took them for crimes they never did.

speaker: Narrator
text: Wooden teeth click together in a ragged plea: cut the boughs, split the heartwood, and let us out.

speaker: Narrator
text: Three faces near the base of the trunk strain forward against the grain, speaking one after another in hushed, splintered breaths. A hollow-cheeked woman claims she only took a loaf of barley bread, while a gaunt man swears the boundary stone was moved before he ever plowed the field.

speaker: Narrator
text: Highest of the three, the broad, scarred likeness of Gory Gus groans through a split lip, begging you to hack him free of the sap before the tree drinks the last of his name.

speaker: Narrator
text: The great boughs groan like a gallows under weight, and the roots wrench themselves from the soil of the Round in a shower of cold dirt and sour blood.

speaker: Narrator
text: You step back onto the cobblestones, and one by one the wooden eyelids pinch shut until only blind bark remains under the leering moon.

speaker: Narrator
text: A long, warm sigh passes through the shattered trunk as the carved mouths slacken, smoothing back into plain timber one by one until the bark is blind and still.

speaker: Narrator
text: She wraps a parcel of cold mutton fat in butcher's paper with raw, trembling knuckles, keeping her eyes fixed on the sawdust floor.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: Pardon me, strangers, only I saw you looking by the alley gate. When the bell strikes Evening and I take my basket out to the moor road, please do not follow me, and ask no questions.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: Bless you for that, truly. A body needs her own quiet hours when the sickness is so thick in the lanes, and I won't forget your kindness.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Martha does ten hours of honest boning and scrubbing without a complaint, and what she carries home in her bucket at night is her own affair. Leave the woman be.

speaker: Narrator
text: From the gorse bushes down-wind, you watch her drop the basket of bloody trimmings at the treeline, where her spine lengthens with a wet crack and coarse grey fur swallows her shawl.

speaker: Narrator
text: A twig snaps underfoot in the damp heather, and the half-changed thing by the stone wall lifts a long, wet muzzle to the wind.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: Don't look at me, I begged you not to look! The butcher's offal keeps the worst of the hunger down, I swear I never touched a soul!

speaker: Narrator
text: She scrambles over the turf dike on all fours, her torn apron catching on the briars as she vanishes into the dark.

speaker: Narrator
text: She stands behind the chopping block with her sleeves pinned neat to the wrist, though the scent of wet moorland fur still clings to her woollen skirt.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: You know what I am now, and one word to the constable puts my head by the Oak. Tell me plain what you mean to do with me.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: May the Patient Lady shade your steps. As long as I have the trough scraps before the moon climbs, the beast stays fed and the village stays safe.

speaker: Narrator
text: Siv listens with his cleaver resting flat on the oak block, wipes his hands on his apron, and slides a double bucket of marrow bones toward her feet.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Thought it was a stray hound I heard by the smokehouse all winter. Take the beef shins too, Martha, and see you're back before the morning cart.

speaker: Narrator
text: Tears spill down her cheeks onto the salted boards as she presses a knotted handkerchief of silver coins into your palm.

speaker: mrs_oakum
text: I had given up praying to wake from a night without blood in my teeth. Take what little I've saved, and Godspeed to you.

speaker: Narrator
text: Birch twigs scrape across cold cobbles in a slow, steady rhythm. Old Rusty peers out from a tangle of red-grey hair, smelling of damp leaves and hearth smoke.

speaker: old_rusty
text: Step on a crack, break the moon's back. Wipe your boots before you tread the Round, strangers.

speaker: old_rusty
text: Leaves fall down, faces look down. What do you want with an old broom?

speaker: old_rusty
text: Sweep the stone, keep the bone. The village feeds the belly, the broom feeds the square, and the dirt never sleeps.

speaker: old_rusty
text: The stone man has no face to lie with. The old oak has too many, and every one of them is thirsty when the axe comes down.

speaker: old_rusty
text: Six chimes from the tower, one for each hour. When the antlers grow on the little brown hare, lock your shutter and say your prayer.

speaker: Narrator
text: His knuckles whiten on the ash handle whenever his gaze drifts toward the crooked gable high on the ridge. An old white scar splits his scalp beneath the wild hair.

speaker: old_rusty
text: Crooked beam, crooked stair, nobody left to sit in the chair. Don't go up the hill, don't knock on the door.

speaker: old_rusty
text: Wind in the gorse, nothing worse. Mind where you put your heels, I just swept there.

speaker: Narrator
text: Warm beeswax and dried lavender sweeten the cramped shop. A red-haired man wheels his chair smoothly down a pegged timber ramp, grinning from ear to ear.

speaker: oswick_frey
text: Mind your shins on the tallow-vats and welcome! I am Wick Frey, and if it burns on a string, I dip it.

speaker: oswick_frey
text: Now then, what brings fresh faces under my rafters?

speaker: oswick_frey
text: Ritual tapers are free to the Old Ways faithful, mind, though strangers pay in coin for good mutton-fat and beeswax.

speaker: oswick_frey
text: Built the chair with the wheelwright and rigged the pulley to the roof myself. From up top, you can watch every lantern round the Founder's Round.

speaker: oswick_frey
text: Everyone needs light in a land without dawn. Even Master F-Finneas from the schoolhouse stops by for reading candles, when his ink runs low.

speaker: Narrator
text: A dozen spare tapers on his workbench are wrapped in neat paper tied with twine, each marked with the schoolmaster's initial.

speaker: oswick_frey
text: You saw those, did you? Finneas reads till his eyes ache, so I pour him the smokeless clover-wax, though my tongue knots up whenever he thanks me.

speaker: oswick_frey
text: A man likes to keep an eye on the square, that is all. Best seat in Wickermoor for catching the gossip.

speaker: Narrator
text: High in the dusty rafters above the sorting tables, something heavy shifts among the cobwebs. Pink, hairless human fingers curl tightly round the timber beam where claws ought to be, and a pair of jug-handle ears twitch on either side of a feathered skull.

speaker: Narrator
text: The grotesque pigeon leans down into the lantern glow, its greasy feathers smelling of wet wool and attic dust. A wet, throaty coo rumbles from its crop before a splat of white lime drops onto {name}'s shoulder, folded neatly like a tiny note.

speaker: Narrator
text: The fleshy ears flatten against the grey plumage, and its knuckles drum a slow, knowing tap against the oak beam. It points one stubby forefinger toward the postmaster's locked drawer, then shrinks back into the shadow.

speaker: Narrator
text: The bird snaps its beak with a dry clack, scratches one human ear with a calloused thumb, and turns its tail to you.

speaker: george_hickock
text: Good folk, take a bench before the greasepaint dries! Tonight Hickock and Company present The Prince in Gold, a tragedy of crowns and treachery, right here on the inn stage.

speaker: Narrator
text: Behind the painted canvas, Barnaby Quill slumps cold in his chair, a tin goblet rolled beside his boot and a bitter almond scent rising from his velvet collar.

speaker: alda_farnum
text: Saints preserve us, he was supposed to go on at the bell, not lie there stiff in my back room!

speaker: george_hickock
text: Dead, our finest villain dead before the curtain rises! Some fiend has poisoned poor Barnaby, and the whole taproom is waiting for their tragedy!

speaker: lilian_vale
text: Why are you staring at me as if I brewed the stuff? Yes, the scoundrel fleeced me of six silver crowns at cards an hour ago, and now I will never see a penny of it!

speaker: olwen_pike
text: Mind where you tread, the hem of this royal cloak is fray enough without heavy boots on it. Barnaby liked his drink, and nobody kept count of what he poured.

speaker: Narrator
text: At the mention of the cup, her thumb slips against the needle and she draws the thread tight with rapid, jerky stitches.

speaker: olwen_pike
text: A prop is just a prop until an actor makes a mess of it.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her needle dips and rises through the gold braid in a steady, unbroken rhythm, never missing a stitch.

speaker: Narrator
text: The battered tin goblet bears a dab of yellow paint on its base to mark it for the prop table, and its rim is still tacky with sweet, dark dregs.

speaker: Narrator
text: Tucked inside his waistcoat is a torn scrap of paper, demanding payment of an old debt to a woman named Mara before the company leaves the moor.

speaker: george_hickock
text: Speak plainly, friends, if you know whose hand brought ruin to our stage.

speaker: george_hickock
text: Lilian, my star, tell me you did not trade our leading villain for a handful of card money!

speaker: lilian_vale
text: Oh, spare me your grand speeches, George, you cannot pin a murder on me without a shred of proof!

speaker: Narrator
text: Olwen sets her needle neatly into the pincushion and folds the heavy cloak across her lap.

speaker: olwen_pike
text: Mara was the sweetest voice we ever had, until Barnaby took her savings and left her to rot in a debtor's ditch. I set the banquet cup by his elbow, and he drank it greedy as ever.

speaker: george_hickock
text: A dark deed, yet the lanterns are lit and the benches are full! Take up Barnaby's cloak and read his lines, I beg you, or Hickock and Company is finished!

speaker: Narrator
text: You stumble over a verse or two with the script hidden in your sleeve, though the tavern crowd claps heartily enough when the cardboard crown hits the boards.

speaker: Narrator
text: You snarl the villain's curses to the rafters, and the whole taproom rises in a roar of boots and tankards as the curtain falls.

speaker: george_hickock
text: Bravo, my newfound players, a triumph worthy of the grandest halls!

speaker: Narrator
text: The candles along the stage are pinched out one by one, leaving the smell of tallow and cold dust while the actors pack their trunks in silence.

speaker: Narrator
text: A chain and a padlock hold the gate, and a board nailed across it says BY ORDER OF THE MAYOR. On the step behind lies one small child's shoe, laces still tied.

speaker: Narrator
text: The house leans over a lane of empty ones. When you look at its windows, it seems to have been looking at you a moment before.

speaker: Narrator
text: Nobody who lives on the lane will say it plainly. A woman at her gate says the children dare each other, a boy at the inn says the house has more rooms inside than it has outside, and everyone says the shoe belongs to somebody.

speaker: Narrator
text: The padlock gives with a dull crack. The gate swings an inch, and something in the house breathes in, long and slow.

speaker: Narrator
text: The shoe on the step is gone. Behind you, in the lane, a child laughs, and nobody is there. You pull the gate shut and press the chain back round it, and it feels like the right thing to have done.

speaker: Narrator
text: The chain does not budge, and the house seems to settle a little, pleased.

speaker: Narrator
text: A scrap of herb-stained parchment hangs crookedly from the apothecary door, smelling faintly of crushed mint.

speaker: morgan
text: If anyone has a spare moment, a pedlar in the Round is selling a plague cure. I cannot leave the kettle, so please see what is in it, and whether it does harm.

speaker: Narrator
text: You fold the note into your coat while the pestle keeps up its tired rhythm inside.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
text: Step lively, good neighbours, and fortify your humours with Pennywhistle's Sovereign Specific. Every green bottle carries a fresh guarantee against the creeping itch, or your brass Cheerfully refunded.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
text: Now, I could hardly hand over my sainted grandmother's receipt in the open damp. Call it forty mountain herbs steeped under a lucky star, and leave the arithmetic to me.

speaker: Narrator
text: The cork gives with a sticky pop, releasing a warm, unmistakable waft of cellar cider and cheap cinnamon.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
text: A wise investment for troubled times, friend, and do remember to shake the sediment before supper.

speaker: Narrator
text: Barnaby straightens his cuffs by the crate of clinking bottles, watching the crowd with bright, restless eyes.

speaker: Narrator
text: Beneath the sweet orchard cider and cinnamon bark sits a bitter trace of boiled willow and wildflower honey. It will cure no plague, though it might soothe a feverish throat and warm a cold belly.

speaker: Narrator
text: The draught burns pleasantly across your tongue with fierce cinnamon and sour apples, masking whatever else might be floating at the bottom.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
text: You have a terribly solemn look about you, traveller, and solemnity is dreadful for the digestion.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
text: Keep your voice down, I beg you, before the sick folk lose their temper. It is mulled cider, willow bark for the aches, and a spoonful of honey to keep their spirits from sinking.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
text: Bless your heart, I have faced louder bailiffs in three counties and sold them all hair tonic. Take two bottles for three coins and spare us both the frown.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
text: Well, you have the measure of my little kettle now. A drop of warmth and willow tea is better than cold panic, so what do you mean to do with me?

speaker: Narrator
text: Word travels fast around the blankets, and within moments a chorus of coughing townsfolk is pelting Barnaby's cart toward the gate with turnip tops.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
text: Ungrateful hamlet, upon my word! May your joints stay draughty and your tea go cold!

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
text: You have a gentle soul beneath that travel dust, friend. Take the best bottle from the bottom row for the apothecary, and take this coin for keeping a quiet tongue.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
text: Now there is a head for honest commerce in a dark season. Stand beside the crate looking healthy, nod when I mention the forty herbs, and we shall split the evening's tin.

speaker: barnaby_pennywhistle
text: No offence meant, my dear colleague, but a trade secret shared with four strangers is just a recipe on a tavern wall.

speaker: Narrator
text: The bottle smells of cider and cinnamon.

speaker: Narrator
text: Stacks of damp parchment lean across the mayor's desk like toppling gravestones, smelling faintly of boiled vinegar and sealing wax.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Dreadful business, friends, dreadful! Half the parish is coughing up centipedes in the taproom, yet I cannot legally bar the inn doors without three county seals in triplicate.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: My hands are tied with red ribbon while the kettle boils over. Would you take the sheaf to Miss Ledger and Miss Mayville for their stamps?

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Why, one for the parish chest, one for the post bag, and one nailed to the Oak so the Green Queen sees we did things properly.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Nobody remembers which magistrate wrote the statute, only that an unsealed plague is an unlawful plague.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Bless your brisk boots! Mind the ink does not smudge in the fog, or Miss Ledger will make us start from the first sheet.

speaker: Narrator
text: Tamsin Ledger wets her thumb and turns a fresh page, her spectacles gleaming like two brass coins in the lantern light.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
text: Form Seven-B, Emergency Pestilence and Bedstead Tally. What a treat! I can countersign the second copy the moment we verify the active cots in the common room.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
text: Fourteen feverish, three merely twitching, and two sharing a bolster. Everything reconciles to the half-column.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her iron stamp comes down with a crisp, joyful thud that rattles the inkwell.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
text: Fifteen? No, no, the drover under the settle is only sleeping off turnip gin. I have struck him from the pestilence column in red ink.

speaker: tamsin_ledger
text: There. Nothing warms the blood like a corrected ledger.

speaker: Narrator
text: Behind the wicket, Theodora Mayville sorts dead letters with a bone knife, her head tilting in sharp, birdlike jerks.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: The Mayor's quarantine circulars. Set them by the brass scale and do not breathe on the gummed edges. I stamp emergency notices after the afternoon sorting.

speaker: Narrator
text: She fixes you with a round, unblinking stare and drives the postmark into the wax with a single sharp peck of her wrist.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: Properly witnessed, properly weighed. Take your papers off my counter before you shed road grit into the pigeonholes.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: Haste is how envelopes lose their corners. Come back when the kettle has cooled and I have finished the dead-letter bundle.

speaker: Narrator
text: While her back is turned to the sorting rack, {name} rolls a carved cork in purple ink and presses three neat rings across the parchment.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: Hmph. Still standing there? Keep your elbows off the blotter.

speaker: Narrator
text: A heavy gloved hand closes on {name}'s wrist just as the counterfeit stamp leaves a smeared purple crescent on the page.

speaker: doris_squire
text: Counterfeiting the parish postmark during a pestilence. Keep the smudged copy for the Mayor, and bring your boots to the cells until morning.

speaker: Narrator
text: Wendel presses his own brass signet into the warm wax, then holds all three sheets up to the hearth like prize marrow squashes.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Three ribbons, nine stamps, and not a single blot on the margin! Now the village may be Deathly Ill in full compliance with the bylaws.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Take this for your shoe-leather, friends, and step lively around the inn porch.

speaker: ambrose_quill
text: Ah, fresh ears in the Green Queen's taproom! I am Ambrose Quill, humble vessel of the muse, paring eternity down to metre and ink.

speaker: ambrose_quill
text: Dark blows the wind through Wickermoor, where misty lanterns shine so bright. We bolt the heavy timber door, and drink our ale until Tuesday.

speaker: ambrose_quill
text: Notice how the final word defies expectation. Rhyme is a cage for lesser birds.

speaker: ambrose_quill
text: Beneath the boughs of ancient oak, the carved faces watch the folk. They drink the red rain under oak, and never once let out a spoke.

speaker: ambrose_quill
text: Pairing oak with oak gives the stanza a sturdy, rooted symmetry, don't you think?

speaker: ambrose_quill
text: Six iron bells inside the tower, strike the grim and nameless hour. Cold brass gears that grind and clank, like turnips tumbling down a bank.

speaker: ambrose_quill
text: We wear the names we had before, though half the letters washed away. The dead knock softly at the door, and ask who lived here yesterday.

speaker: ambrose_quill
text: Hm. Too simple, perhaps. It lacks the grandeur of the turnip image.

speaker: ambrose_quill
text: Mayor Somerton commissioned an anthem for the Founders' table, yet the village's own name resists my craft. What mortal tongue can rhyme with Wickermoor?

speaker: Narrator
text: You rack your brains around the table, and the best anyone can offer is 'floor more'.

speaker: ambrose_quill
text: Floor more! Inspired! A double-barrelled chime of domestic abundance! Consider it immortalised.

speaker: Narrator
text: Sharp white spirit, bay rum, and warm soap mingle in the little parlour. A burly sandy-bearded man strops a razor with an easy, neighbourly grin.

speaker: randall_graham
text: Well now, fresh faces in the hollow! Sit yourselves down for a trim, a stitch, or a splash of my own clear shine to chase the damp out.

speaker: randall_graham
text: Take a weight off your boots, friends. Randall's chair is always open.

speaker: randall_graham
text: Hold still and breathe easy, my hand is the steadiest in Wickermoor and the jug is right beside the basin.

speaker: randall_graham
text: A village this size needs one fellow to trim beards, pull bad molars, and sew up a split brow. Folks talk freer with a warm towel round their chin.

speaker: randall_graham
text: You should look in on young Thomasin the tailor, a bright soul who listens well to old wisdom. This hollow remembers its roots deeper than the city folk think.

speaker: randall_graham
text: They say the old powers in the woods are stirring under the crone's moon, hungry for what was stolen from them. Best keep on the right side of the forest.

speaker: Narrator
text: Nicked into the wood under the second chair's arm is a tiny hare crowned with antlers, and Randall nudges a lock of clipped hair away from your boot.

speaker: randall_graham
text: Ah, step clear of the clippings, friend, it brings sour luck to let a customer's hair blow out the door. Everything trimmed under my roof stays safe downstairs.

speaker: Narrator
text: Randall sweeps the floorboards into a lidded pail with a single brisk stroke of his broom.

speaker: randall_graham
text: Nothing to see on the floor but split ends and moor dust, friend.

speaker: Narrator
text: He stands by the heavy timber post like part of the framing, smelling of pipe tallow and wet wool.

speaker: ronald_wainwright
text: Evening to you. Mind the step by the barrels, the wood stays slick.

speaker: ronald_wainwright
text: I am right here if you need pointing somewhere.

speaker: ronald_wainwright
text: Wilma tells me where to stand, and I stand there until the bell changes. Most folks behave once they see the pair of us.

speaker: ronald_wainwright
text: It is a quiet hollow if you leave the old trees be and honour the Green Queen. The Oak in the Round has watched over worse nights than this.

speaker: ronald_wainwright
text: Zachariah whittled a wooden hare yesterday and Eddie tried to trade it to Mr. Tolliver for peppermints. Good lads, and Victoria keeps them in line.

speaker: Narrator
text: Braided oak twine and three small wooden tokens hang inside his cuff, polished smooth by his thumb.

speaker: ronald_wainwright
text: One knot for each child down in the cellar, prayed over at the Founder's Round. A man cannot watch every shadow, so he asks the Queen to watch too.

speaker: ronald_wainwright
text: Just an old wool coat, friend. Keeps the moor chill off my shoulders.

speaker: Narrator
text: You catch the low murmur of a drover warming his chapped hands over a brazier of damp peat. He swears a cooper's lad up the lane opened his mouth to say grace and spoke instead in the rusted, grating baritone of a long-dead magistrate.

speaker: Narrator
text: Two women in woollen shawls trade sharp whispers over a basket of bruised turnips, their breath misting in the cold. One vows her neighbour put the evil eye on her dairy, turning a whole wheel of sweet cream cheese green and weeping with maggots.

speaker: Narrator
text: A tinker nursing a mug of sour cider leans toward the hearth, lowering his voice so the barkeep will not hear. He claims three toddlers in the outer cottages have grown coarse grey bristles along their spines and taken to gnawing raw marrow bones under the beds.

speaker: Narrator
text: By the well, a watchman rubs his aching knees and grumbles about a series of peculiar break-ins across the parish. The thief leaves silver spoons and coin purses untouched, taking only family Bibles, baby teeth from keepsake boxes, and locks of hair clipped from sleeping folk.

speaker: Narrator
text: You overhear a woodcutter telling his trembling apprentice to stay clear of the high bracken after the third bell. They found a shepherd standing upright in the gorse with his eyes wide open and cold as river stones, his chest empty of breath while something pale loped into the fog.

speaker: Narrator
text: Behind the stables, two carters pass a clay pipe back and forth, speaking of strangers with gold-leaf rings and oiled blades. Folks say a secret brotherhood of misers in the valley pays those quiet knives to slit the throats of debtors and weigh their hearts against brass scales.

speaker: Narrator
text: An old woman shelling peas on her stoop mutters to her cat about the barefoot penitents gathering up on the tors. They smear their faces with mutton tallow and ash, howling prayers to hurry the end of the world before the moon can shut her watchful eye.

speaker: Narrator
text: A gravedigger scraping mud from his spade tells the sexton about the corpse they carried in from the crossroad ditch. The dead man's hair had turned snow-white from terror, and they had to crack his stiff knuckles with a mallet to pry a cold marble finger from his fist.

speaker: Narrator
text: Two washerwomen wringing out linen sheets gossip about a wealthy widow who bolted her shutters at the start of the month. The milkman smelled brimstone and burnt sugar through her keyhole, and saw a tall suitor in velvet cuffs whose shadow wore a pair of curled horns.

speaker: Narrator
text: Near the lychgate, a choirboy whispers to his sister while tossing dry crusts onto the frost. He says the bluebirds nesting in the rafters never sing during hymns anymore, only cock their bright heads to listen when sinners confess and tap the windowpanes in three-beat riddles.

speaker: Narrator
text: A drover leaning on the paddock rail points a scarred thumb toward the black ridge beyond the moor. Every night the wind carries the reek of pine tar and scorching wool from distant bonfires, keeping time with skin drums that thud like a giant's slow heartbeat.

speaker: Narrator
text: Over the clatter of pewter plates, a seamstress tells the chandler about the teenagers who wandered back from the hazel copse. They sit in the mud braiding dead nettles into crowns, speaking only in crooked nursery rhymes that make the village hounds whine and crawl under the porch.

speaker: Narrator
text: A trapper smells of wet hound and woodsmoke as he warns the ostler away from the northern marsh. His own brother came back from the reeds without his rifle or his tongue's old cunning, only whistling four wet, reed-thin notes whenever someone speaks his name.

speaker: Narrator
text: Two weavers waiting by the fuller's vats compare the sour taste in their mouths after waking from the very same nightmare. Half the lane dreamed of climbing a ladder of braided silver frost into the black sky, where cold stars sang to them like choirs of glass.

speaker: Narrator
text: A dockhand spits into the gutter and warns a passing peddler never to buy meat pasties from the cellar bakehouse after dark. He swears he found a long, scaly tail baked into the lard crust, though the pepper gravy was rich enough to make him eat a second.

speaker: Narrator
text: Down by the weir, an angler mending his hemp net swears the river is growing crowded with things that are not trout. He saw pale, webbed hands gripping the slick stones below the millwheel, and wide yellow eyes blinking up through the brown foam.

speaker: Narrator
text: A ploughman nursing a bandaged thumb tells the smith what his iron share struck in the south fallow field. They dug up a bronze vessel green with verdigris and sealed with human teeth, and since that hour every crow in the parish has circled their chimney.

speaker: Narrator
text: Two girls stringing dried apples by the lantern light speak in hushed voices about last season's harvest queen. Her wreath of wheat and ribbons was found floating in the horse trough at dawn, and nobody has seen hide nor hair of the lass since the feast.

speaker: Narrator
text: An apothecary measuring dried rue tells his customer to cross the street before passing the crooked gable at the end of the lane. The little girl looking out that dusty casement has worn the same pinafore and held the same china doll since his grandfather was a boy.

speaker: Narrator
text: A sweep brushing soot from his sleeves nods up toward the dark belfry above the square. Last week the iron bell struck a seventh, nameless hour in the dead of night, and the old watchmaker and his wife walked hand in hand right off the parapet.

speaker: Narrator
text: The silver sunflower on the preacher's chest catches the bonfire light as she turns, her red hair whipping around her shoulders like autumn leaves.

speaker: sister_rain
text: Blessings of the gentle rain upon your boots, strangers! Come warm your hands and hear how the Patient Lady keeps the seed safe beneath the frost!

speaker: sister_rain
text: The earth doesn't ask for heads on an oak or cages of iron, friends, it only asks for patience and clean rain.

speaker: sister_rain
text: Yet folk here meet every shadow with an axe and a torch, fighting fire with fire until the whole blessed meadow is ash!

speaker: sister_rain
text: Mayor Somerton means well enough in his stiff way, I suppose, though his Old Ways have grown sour and hungry. Then next moment my heart just sings to see a green shoot cracking the stone!

speaker: sister_rain
text: If your feet carry you down the road to Foxwillow, go with a soft word on your tongue. Neighbour has turned against neighbour down there, and their bitter blood is poisoning the creek.

speaker: Narrator
text: Where her fingers brush the mud between the stones, a shudder runs up her arm as though she touched a hot kettle, and the hem of her green dress wilts grey.

speaker: sister_rain
text: Can you not feel it stinging through your soles? Something buried deep under the roots is festering like a rusty nail, and the whole valley's soil is sick with fever.

speaker: Narrator
text: She rises from the mud and dusts her skirt with a sudden, bright laugh, the storm in her green eyes passing as quick as an April shower.

speaker: sister_rain
text: Only checking if the dew has fallen yet. A country girl never trusts the sky without feeling the dirt first.

speaker: Narrator
text: Scrubbed pine tables smell of coarse salt and winter savory, with not a fly in sight. Siv wipes a broad cleaver on clean linen, her heavy blonde braids pinned back from a calm, weathered face.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Good greeting to you. The meat is hung proper and bled clean, if your pack needs provisioning.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Speak what you need. A sharp blade and an honest weight save everyone time.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Salted mutton, smoked bacon, and marrow bones. It will keep you standing on the moor.

speaker: siv_harga
text: I buy from the hill crofters, keep the pens clean out back, and go home to Holly's warm bread and our two girls. A house with flour on the table and meat in the smoke-room lacks very little.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Before the knife touches the throat, I ask the Patient Lady to take the beast's breath gently. The Green Queen wants blood on roots, my Lady only asks that nothing suffer for our supper.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Holly stays at the ovens too late, counting chimes and staring at the calendar chalk. If anyone brings trouble near my door while her heart is heavy, they will meet the cleaver.

speaker: Narrator
text: Behind the shop wall, a penned wether gives a low bleat and presses its wool against the boards at the sound of her voice.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Folks talk foolishness because I keep my voice down and don't beat a frightened sheep. Still, the ewes won't face the northern hills this week, and a sheep knows a wolf with antlers before a man does.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Perhaps the old rams tell me all the parish gossip, and perhaps I just know when a beast has bad teeth.

speaker: Narrator
text: Stone dust hangs thick in the yard, sharp as powdered chalk on your tongue. Solomon sets down a heavy iron mallet and steps between you and a small girl sorting chisels.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Keep your boots off the dressed slate. If you want a headstone or a lintel, speak plain.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: State your business. Daylight never comes, and the stone doesn't cut itself.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Good granite and sound tools. Touch only what you can pay for.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: My crews cut the ridge quarry, and I carve what lasts. Sofia tallies the chalk marks for me, better head for numbers than half my men.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Keep at the ledger, little bird, I'll be right here.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Most folk here kneel to the old tree and the Mayor's Green Queen. Stone outlasts bark, if you ask me, though nobody does.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Young Weston's choir sings of morning and clean hands. When you've got a child to raise under that grinning moon, a song about dawn is worth good coin.

speaker: Narrator
text: His scarred thumb rubs an old chisel mark on his forearm, and his cold brown eyes track a bent shadow by the lane.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Every town has rot under the floorboards. Watch the folk who walk with their necks tilted and smile at the hill, I've seen their master in my sleep since I was Sofia's age.

speaker: solomon_roderick
text: Staring won't lower my prices. Buy what you need or clear the yard.

speaker: Narrator
text: Flour dust hangs thick in the bakery's hot air, smelling of焦ed crust and boiled turnip water.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Half the village is shivering under blankets, and I am boiling turnip skins like a pauper. My bread will fill bellies, sure, but fever needs proper marrow broth.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Siv Harga has a barrel of beef shanks sitting in salt, yet the stubborn ox locks his door when he sees my apron.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Bless your boots. Tell him the kettle is for the sick beds, not a prize ribbon, though he still does not know how to season a crust.

speaker: Narrator
text: Siv's cleaver thuds into the salted tallow of the chopping block, while a fat black centipede curls dead in the sawdust at your feet.

speaker: siv_harga
text: If Holly Aster sent you after my soup bones, you can march right back to her ovens. The Founders' Feast is barely cold, and my pride is not on the clearance hook.

speaker: siv_harga
text: A man's marrow is his craft, strangers, and I do not hand mine over to a woman who measures salt by the pinch.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Bah, take the crate by the door before I find a use for it. Tell her to skim the tallow properly, or I will come down to the Round and do it myself.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Charity is for church mice, not bakers who smirk behind their loaves. Put ten gold on the counter for the weight, or try me when my temper cools.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Ten coin is fair weight for prime knuckle and rib, plague or no plague. Haul them out, and tell Holly the best part of her soup walked out of my shop.

speaker: Narrator
text: Out in the Round, an iron camp stove belches damp oak smoke between two crowded cots.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Move your kettle three inches left, Siv, or my loaves will draw damp from your lid.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Your tin pans are hogging the grate, woman, and broth takes the centre coal or it never clears.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Fine, so long as nobody touches my damper.

speaker: siv_harga
text: Good enough, now pass the ladle and stop hovering over my shanks.

speaker: Narrator
text: Rich beef steam curls across the Founder's Round, cutting through the sour damp of fever blankets.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Look at old Granny Pike taking a full bowl with a crust dipped in. Siv's bones did the trick, though you will never hear me tell him so before Sundown.

speaker: holly_aster
text: Take this from the parish kitty for your trouble, friends. You kept two stubborn fools from starving their neighbours.

speaker: Narrator
text: The post office smells of sealing wax, damp feathers, and old parchment. A fat grey pigeon on the postmaster's shoulder swivels its head to fix you with an unblinking orange eye.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: Welcome to Wickermoor's post, travellers. If you have word for the wider valley, my birds and wagons will see it carried safe.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: A letter is a fragile thing in the dark, isn't it? Folks pour their whole hearts onto a scrap of paper and trust me to mend the distance.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: I read the addresses, bind the twine, and make sure every soul gets the exact message they need to hear.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: Oh, the village is quaint enough, with their bonfires and their precious old oak. They pray so hard to the woods, poor dears, never looking up at what flies overhead.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: Let's see what needs carrying, then. Mind the wax, it's fresh off the flame.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: Folk down the lane complain that answers from distant kin don't sound quite like their loved ones anymore. Grief muddles the memory, I tell them, and the night air changes us all.

speaker: Narrator
text: Beneath the neat calfskin of her left glove, the knuckles bend at an extra, backward joint, stiff and scaly. Beside her ear, the golden pigeon earring gleams as the live bird tracks {name}'s every breath.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: You've a sharp eye, stranger. Best keep it on the road ahead, lest the dust get in it.

speaker: Narrator
text: She smooths her brown apron with her gloved hand, the very picture of a tidy country clerk. The pigeon merely ruffles its crop and settles against her white-blond hair.

speaker: theodora_mayville
text: Did you smudge your sleeve on the inkpot, dear? Do be careful.

speaker: Narrator
text: Pins glint in a velvet cushion, and the room is hushed save for the crisp snip of shears. Thomasin measures your cloak with one cool, unblinking glance.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: Welcome to A Stitch in Time. Wipe the moor-mud from your boots before you step upon the drop-cloth, if you please.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: How may I be of service to you?

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: Look closely at the seams on your travels, and bring me any strange cloth you find. I can mend homespun or cobble a split boot while you wait.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: Those are courtly cuts I drafted for velvet and silver thread. Folk here only ever order grey wool coats and mourning bands.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: Small towns enjoy small tales, and I do not care to chatter at the well. They call me proud, which leaves me peace to sew.

speaker: Narrator
text: Beneath her high lace collar runs a neat, surgical seam across her throat, pinned with a tiny pewter hare bearing antlers.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: I fell through a greenhouse pane as a girl, and Master Randall stitched my life back together. He says his quiet friends have great need of my needle.

speaker: thomasin_ardor
text: It is only an old childhood scratch and a trinket from a kind neighbour. Nothing that concerns a passing customer.

speaker: Narrator
text: Waxed paper and peppermint hair-oil fill the snug office, where the Mayor taps his emerald-headed cane against a stack of fresh forms.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Ah, our distinguished visitors, right on time between Twilight and Nightfall. In here we may dispense with square-side ceremony and attend to proper municipal order.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: I shall say plainly that the village has not forgotten the goat. My people are slow to forgive a spoiled rite, so do mind your manners about town.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: And you will recall what I told you in the Round. The fevers, the empty chairs. Ask what you will; I shall answer as I can.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Every permit stamped, every boundary dispute filed in triplicate, and Lord Phillip shall see a model parish. A village without ledgers is merely a camp in the heather.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: As speaker for the Old Ways, I see that the Green Queen receives her traditional dues and the Oak is respected. The smaller faiths have their little corners, of course, under my benevolent eye.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: I have the official register of permits, deeds, and municipal rewards right here.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Three separate complaints of night-singing near the standing stones, and a petition about blighted turnips. People blame ancient curses when they have simply neglected their drainage ditches.

speaker: Narrator
text: He puffs out his waistcoat, fondling the jewelled oak-leaf pin at his lapel as though reciting someone else's lesson.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: Between ourselves, Alda and young Butterman have been marvelous at unearthing the older rites from the parish chests. They assure me the old horned-hare processions will impress the gentry no end.

speaker: Narrator
text: He straightens his bowler hat on the peg and squares a bundle of parchment with loud taps.

speaker: wendel_somerton
text: A mayor relies on his own seasoned judgment, my friends, and forty years of sound filing.

speaker: Narrator
text: Sawdust and damp mortar scent the half-roofed chapel. A sandy-haired young man lowers his mallet, his smile bright enough to warm the cold stones.

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: Come in, friends, and rest your travel-sore feet! The roof still leaks a bit, but the Brightsingers turn no soul away from the song.

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: Tell me, brothers and sisters, what weighs upon you tonight?

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: Bow your heads and let the Dawn-Bird's grace mend what the dark has bruised. So long as breath remains, no soul is beyond a second verse.

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: My Joan and our little ones, Peter and Charlotte, haul shingles right alongside me. Every nail we drive is a promise that mercy has a home here.

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: Mayor Somerton prefers his old roots and blood-custom, and he looks sideways at our hymns. Still, fearful hearts grow tired of harsh gods.

speaker: Narrator
text: His fingers tighten on the hammer shaft, his knuckles whitening as he looks toward the square where the great carved oak stands.

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: I preach redemption because I must believe in it, friend. My own mother and father died on the headsman's block, and I will not let their sin be my children's heritage.

speaker: weston_murdoch
text: Only a chill draft through the rafters, friend. A man cannot look at that grim tree in the square without wishing for warmer light.

speaker: Narrator
text: Down by the cellar steps smells of boiled cabbage, damp wool, and iron oil. A brisk woman keeps one hand near her club and an ear cocked toward the floorboards.

speaker: wilma_wainwright
text: Wipe your boots before you tread mud across Mr. Tolliver's floorboards. Looking is free, touching is fine, and making trouble answers to Ronald and me.

speaker: wilma_wainwright
text: Speak plain if you need something, I have three youngsters below and soup on the stove.

speaker: wilma_wainwright
text: Mr. Tolliver gives us the basement and an honest wage to mind the post. It keeps a dry roof over Victoria, Eddie, and little Zachariah, Green Queen bless them.

speaker: wilma_wainwright
text: We keep to the Old Ways, bar the shutters at the late bells, and mind the Founder's Round. Strangers who respect custom do well enough here.

speaker: wilma_wainwright
text: Those three little ones lost their folks to what comes at night out on the moor. That is all I am saying with young ears under the boards.

speaker: Narrator
text: Her knuckles whiten on her belt, and her eyes flick toward the six quarters of the valley beyond the walls.

speaker: wilma_wainwright
text: There are six great hungers out in this valley, and they do not leave bones to bury. Keep your lanterns lit if you walk past the stones.

speaker: wilma_wainwright
text: Do not go prying after grief that is none of your business. The children are fed and warm, and that is what counts.
